1Week 1 · Lecture 1

Governing equations and strain measures

Governing equations in statics

A body deforms under the action of forces. How it deforms depends on the applied forces, the geometry of the body and the behaviour of its material. Three families of equations connect them:

  • Equilibrium equations relate stresses to external forces.
  • Constitutive equations relate strains to stresses.
  • Kinematic equations relate displacements to strains.

When the forces are known, we move along the chain forces → stresses → strains → displacements.

Assumptions

Continuum medium. Matter is distributed continuously in the volume occupied by the body, and the body is characterised by macroscopic properties. We care about variations at length scales much larger than those of the microstructure.

Linear model. In this course we assume an infinitesimal placement (small rotations and deformations, so geometry changes are neglected) and linear material behaviour (stresses and strains are related linearly). Both are valid for a wide range of applications, but both have their limits.

Slide example: governing equations

We found a piece of green plastic and run a set of experimental tests on it (traction, compression, bending). Which equations are we trying to determine?

Average strain in 1D

A bar of length \(L\) deforms to length \(\ell = L + \delta\). Two average strain measures over the whole bar:

\[ \epsilon = \frac{\ell - L}{L} = \frac{\delta}{L} \;\;\text{(Cauchy)}, \qquad E = \frac12\,\frac{\ell^2 - L^2}{L^2} \;\;\text{(Green–Lagrange)}. \]

Any strain measure must be dimensionless and must vanish when the deformation vanishes.

Point strain

To characterise deformation at a point we need its position and its surrounding. Mark points \(P\) and \(Q\) a distance \(\Delta X\) apart; with displacements \(u\) and \(u + \Delta u\),

\[ \epsilon_P = \lim_{\Delta X \to 0} \frac{u_Q - u_P}{X_Q - X_P} = \frac{du}{dX}. \]

Motion of a 3D body

Convention: capital letters in the undeformed configuration, small letters in the deformed one. Point \(P\) at \(\mathbf X\) moves to \(p\) at \(\mathbf x = \mathbf X + \mathbf u\), and a line element \(d\mathbf X\) maps to

\[ d\mathbf x = d\mathbf X + d\mathbf u = d\mathbf X + \frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}\, d\mathbf X, \qquad du_1 = \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial X_1}dX_1 + \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial X_2}dX_2 + \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial X_3}dX_3. \]

The Green–Lagrange strain tensor

Looking at the change in length of \(d\mathbf X\) and working out the algebra gives

\[ \|d\mathbf x\|^2 - \|d\mathbf X\|^2 = 2\, d\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\, d\mathbf X, \qquad \mathbf E = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X} + \frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}^{\mathsf T}\right) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}^{\mathsf T}\frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}. \]

In index notation,

\[ E_{ij} = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial X_j} + \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial X_i}\right) + \frac12\sum_{k=1}^{3}\frac{\partial u_k}{\partial X_i}\frac{\partial u_k}{\partial X_j}, \qquad E_{11} = \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial X_1} + \frac12\left[\left(\frac{\partial u_1}{\partial X_1}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial u_2}{\partial X_1}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial u_3}{\partial X_1}\right)^2\right]. \]

\(\mathbf E\) measures deformation with respect to the undeformed configuration, is entirely determined by the displacement gradients, and is symmetric with 6 independent components. Strain is a second-order tensor: defined by a magnitude and two directions.

Slide example: kinematic equations

A block undergoes the placement \(x_1 = X_1 + \tfrac13 X_2,\; x_2 = X_2\). What is the deformed configuration?

2Week 2 · Lecture 2

Study and use of strain tensors

As a body deforms, a small cube changes in two ways: its sides change length, and its right angles change. The components of the strain tensor describe exactly these two effects.

Change in length in a specific direction

With a unit vector \(\mathbf M = d\mathbf X/\|d\mathbf X\|\) along the line element, dividing by \(\|d\mathbf X\|^2\) gives the Green–Lagrange strain in the direction of \(\mathbf M\):

\[ E_M = \mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\,\mathbf M = \frac12\left(\frac{\|d\mathbf x\|^2}{\|d\mathbf X\|^2} - 1\right), \qquad \|d\mathbf x\| = \sqrt{1 + 2E_M}\,\|d\mathbf X\|. \]

Change in angle between two directions

Two line elements along \(\mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf N\) make an angle \(\Phi\) before and \(\varphi\) after deformation:

\[ \cos\varphi = \frac{\cos\Phi + 2\,\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\,\mathbf N}{\sqrt{1 + 2E_M}\,\sqrt{1 + 2E_N}}. \]

Interpreting the components

Taking \(\mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf N\) along the axes:

\[ E_{11} = \frac12\left(\frac{dx_1^2}{dX_1^2} - 1\right), \qquad \cos\varphi_{12} = \frac{2E_{12}}{\sqrt{1 + 2E_{11}}\,\sqrt{1 + 2E_{22}}}. \]

Diagonal terms measure changes in length of line elements originally along \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3\). Off-diagonal terms measure changes in the angles between them.

Infinitesimal placement

\(\mathbf E\) has linear and quadratic dependencies on the displacement gradient. The quadratic terms are essential when deformations or rotations become finite or large: strings, membranes, buckling.

When a body deforms only slightly and its supports prevent large rotations, the quadratic terms are negligible and derivatives with respect to \(\mathbf X\) or \(\mathbf x\) are equivalent. This gives the Cauchy strain tensor:

\[ \boldsymbol\epsilon = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf x} + \frac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf x}^{\mathsf T}\right), \qquad \epsilon_{ij} = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right). \]

With \(\varphi = \pi/2 - \gamma\) and small strains, \(\cos\varphi = \sin\gamma \approx \gamma\), so the change in angle is

\[ \gamma = 2\,\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\epsilon\,\mathbf N, \qquad \gamma_{12} = 2\epsilon_{12}, \quad \gamma_{23} = 2\epsilon_{23}, \quad \gamma_{13} = 2\epsilon_{13}. \]

Measuring deformation: strain gauges

A strain gauge is glued to the body and deforms with it. In tension its wire gets longer, in compression shorter; the change in resistance is read as a strain in one specific direction, \(E_M = \mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\,\mathbf M\). Gauges in several directions (a rosette) determine the in-plane strain components.

Slide example: measuring deformation

A gauge oriented along \(\mathbf M = \mathbf e_1\) reads \(E_M = 4a\). Which component can we determine?

3Week 3 · Lecture 3

Equilibrium equations: stress measures

Mechanical stress is an abstraction of the intensity of interatomic and intermolecular forces. Under the continuum hypothesis it measures the average intensity of internal forces, with the dimension of force per unit area (N/m² or Pa). It is used to assess resistance to permanent deformation or rupture and to set safety factors.

Global equilibrium of a body

Two kinds of loads act on a body: forces per unit volume \(\rho\mathbf f\) (N/m³, with \(\mathbf f\) per unit mass and \(\rho\) the density) on its volume \(v\), and forces per unit area \(\mathbf q\) (N/m²) on the part \(a_q\) of its outer surface. Supports on \(a_u\) exert reaction forces \(\mathbf r\), with \(a_u \cap a_q = \varnothing\).

\[ \mathbf F_O = \int_v \rho\mathbf f\,dv + \int_{a_q}\mathbf q\,da = \mathbf 0, \qquad \mathbf M_O = \int_v \mathbf x\times\rho\mathbf f\,dv + \int_{a_q}\mathbf x\times\mathbf q\,da = \mathbf 0. \]

Three equilibrium equations in translation and three in rotation.

Cutting a body

Each part of a body in equilibrium is itself in equilibrium. Cutting with a plane \(\Pi\) into a left part \(L\) and right part \(R\) exposes internal forces: \(\mathbf p^L\) exerted by the left part on the right and \(\mathbf p^R\) by the right on the left. By action/reaction they are equal and opposite, and the internal forces on one part are equivalent to the external forces acting on the other part.

Stress vector

\[ \mathbf p = \lim_{\Delta a \to 0}\frac{\Delta\mathbf F_O}{\Delta a}. \]

The stress vector depends on the position of the point and on the orientation of the facet, given by its outward unit normal \(\mathbf n\). For normals \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3\) we write \(\mathbf p_1, \mathbf p_2, \mathbf p_3\), and \(\mathbf p_{-i} = -\mathbf p_i\).

Stress state at a point

Equilibrium of a small tetrahedron (with \(da_i = n_i\,da\) and the volume term negligible since \(dv \ll da\)) shows that the stress vectors at a point are not independent:

\[ \mathbf p = \mathbf p_1 n_1 + \mathbf p_2 n_2 + \mathbf p_3 n_3 = \boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n = \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{21} & \sigma_{31}\\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{22} & \sigma_{32}\\ \sigma_{13} & \sigma_{23} & \sigma_{33}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}n_1\\ n_2\\ n_3\end{bmatrix}. \]

\(\boldsymbol\sigma\) is the Cauchy stress tensor: a second-order tensor with 9 components. The dependence on position and orientation is decoupled: \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) depends only on position. Row \(i\) holds the components of \(\mathbf p_i\): \(\mathbf p_1 = \sigma_{11}\mathbf e_1 + \sigma_{12}\mathbf e_2 + \sigma_{13}\mathbf e_3\).

Slide example: stress vector and tensor

A wedge’s top surface makes \(30^\circ\) with the horizontal. At \(Q\) on that surface, \(\boldsymbol\sigma = a\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt3 & 0 & 3\sqrt3\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ 3\sqrt3 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\). Which is the stress vector on the top surface?

Normal and shear stress

In composites or at contacts we care about stress in specific directions. The stress vector splits into a normal part along \(\mathbf n\) and a shear part in the facet:

\[ \boldsymbol\sigma_n = (\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p)\,\mathbf n, \quad \sigma = \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p, \qquad \boldsymbol\sigma_\tau = \mathbf p - \boldsymbol\sigma_n, \quad \tau^2 = \mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p - \sigma^2. \]

Principal stresses and directions

There is a frame \(\{\mathbf n_1, \mathbf n_2, \mathbf n_3\}\) in which \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) is diagonal: only normal stresses act, so \(\mathbf p = \sigma\mathbf n\). This is an eigenvalue problem:

\[ \left(\boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T} - \sigma\mathbf I\right)\mathbf n = \mathbf 0, \qquad \det\left(\boldsymbol\sigma - \sigma\mathbf I\right) = 0. \]

A symmetric tensor has three real principal values; if they are distinct, the principal directions are orthogonal.

Lab: stress vector on a facet

Set a 2D stress state and rotate the facet normal \(\mathbf n\). The lab computes \(\mathbf p = \boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n\) and splits it into normal and shear parts. When \(\mathbf n\) lines up with a principal direction (dashed), the shear vanishes and \(\mathbf p\) is parallel to \(\mathbf n\), as in Week 3, Exercise 1.

Principal stresses and directions help visualise how stress flows through a structure and can inform design, in engineered and natural structures alike.

Special states are recognised by their principal stresses. Line stress: two principal stresses are zero (bars). Plane stress: one principal stress is zero (thin plates).

4Week 4 · Lecture 4

Equilibrium equations: equilibrium stress/force

A body is in equilibrium if it is not moving or only undergoes a uniform translation. Equilibrium equations relate external forces, internal forces and stresses. We assume infinitesimal strain and study the body in its deformed configuration.

Equilibrium in the volume: translation

A small block \(dx_1\,dx_2\,dx_3\) carries \(\rho\mathbf f\) on its volume and stresses on its six facets. On the positive facets the stresses differ slightly: \(\sigma^\star_{ij} = \sigma_{ij} + d\sigma_{ij}\), with \(d\sigma_{11} = \tfrac{\partial\sigma_{11}}{\partial x_1}dx_1\) and so on.

Summing forces along \(\mathbf e_1\) and dividing by the arbitrary volume \(dx_1dx_2dx_3\):

\[ \frac{\partial\sigma_{11}}{\partial x_1} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{21}}{\partial x_2} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{31}}{\partial x_3} + \rho f_1 = 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{3}\frac{\partial\sigma_{ji}}{\partial x_j} + \rho f_i = 0 \quad \forall\mathbf x\in v,\; i = 1,2,3. \]

Equilibrium in the volume: rotation

Taking moments about an axis through the block’s centre parallel to \(\mathbf e_1\) and neglecting higher-order terms leaves \(\sigma_{23} - \sigma_{32} = 0\). Repeating for the other axes:

\[ \sigma_{ij} = \sigma_{ji} \quad \forall\mathbf x\in v. \]

Equilibrium in rotation means the Cauchy stress tensor is symmetric.

Equilibrium at the outer surface

A small tetrahedron \(OABC\) whose facet \(ABC\) lies on the outer surface gives \(\mathbf q = \mathbf p_1 n_1 + \mathbf p_2 n_2 + \mathbf p_3 n_3\). With \(\mathbf p_i = \boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf e_i\), the boundary conditions are

\[ q_i = \sum_{j=1}^{3}\sigma_{ji}n_j \quad \forall\mathbf x\in a_q, \qquad q_1 = \sigma_{11}n_1 + \sigma_{21}n_2 + \sigma_{31}n_3. \]

Slide example: equilibrium at the outer surface

A roadside marker’s rounded top carries a downward force per unit length \(q\). At the point where the normal makes \(45^\circ\), equilibrium along \(\mathbf e_2\) reads \(aq = b\sigma_{12} + c\sigma_{22}\). Find \(a, b, c\).

Exercise sheet week 4 – final answers
  1. All derivatives vanish and \(\rho\mathbf f = \mathbf 0\), so volume equilibrium holds; \(\boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n = \mathbf q\) on every face. Left facet of \(\Pi\): \(\mathbf p = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}[a\;0\;0]^{\mathsf T}\); right facet: \(\mathbf p = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}[a\;0\;0]^{\mathsf T}\).
  2. \(\tfrac{\partial\sigma_{xy}}{\partial x} + \tfrac{\partial\sigma_{yy}}{\partial y} + \tfrac{\partial\sigma_{zy}}{\partial z} + \rho f_y = 0\); \(f_y = -3(a + 4bL)\); \(a\) in force per unit mass, \(b\) in force per unit mass and length.

  4. Face A: \(\sigma_{31} = \sigma_{32} = \sigma_{33} = 0\). Face B: \(\sigma_{11} = q\), \(\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{13} = 0\). The region behind the groove needs attention: smallest cross-section, highest stresses.

5Week 5 · Lecture 5

Constitutive equations: material laws

Constitutive equations relate stresses and strains, and depend on the material. A tensile test on a steel bar (\(\sigma = F/A\) against \(\epsilon = \delta/L\)) shows a linear elastic region: linear because stress is proportional to strain, elastic because the material returns to its initial configuration when unloaded. A reversible material is called conservative.

Assumptions for the rest of the course: continuum, infinitesimal strain, elasticity (reversible behaviour) and linearity. Many materials depart from this significantly.

Hooke’s law and strain energy

In 1D, \(\sigma = E\epsilon\) for \(\sigma < \sigma_Y\), with \(E\) the Young’s modulus. The strain energy density (energy per unit volume to deform the material) is

\[ u = \tfrac12\sigma\epsilon \;\;(1\text{D}), \qquad u = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^3\sum_{j=1}^3\sigma_{ij}\epsilon_{ij} = \tfrac12\left(\sigma_{11}\epsilon_{11} + \sigma_{22}\epsilon_{22} + \sigma_{33}\epsilon_{33} + 2\sigma_{12}\epsilon_{12} + 2\sigma_{23}\epsilon_{23} + 2\sigma_{31}\epsilon_{31}\right). \]

With Voigt notation \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_V = [\epsilon_{11}\;\epsilon_{22}\;\epsilon_{33}\;2\epsilon_{12}\;2\epsilon_{23}\;2\epsilon_{31}]^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\boldsymbol\sigma_V = [\sigma_{11}\;\sigma_{22}\;\sigma_{33}\;\sigma_{12}\;\sigma_{23}\;\sigma_{31}]^{\mathsf T}\), \(u = \tfrac12\boldsymbol\sigma_V^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\epsilon_V\). Careful: other notations exist.

Generalised Hooke’s law

\[ \sigma_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^3\sum_{l=1}^3 C_{ijkl}\,\epsilon_{kl}, \qquad \boldsymbol\sigma_V = \mathbf C\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_V, \qquad u = \tfrac12\boldsymbol\epsilon_V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf C\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_V \ge 0. \]

Of the 81 components of the fourth-order tensor \(\mathbf C\), symmetry of stress, symmetry of strain and the existence of \(u\) leave 21 independent ones for an anisotropic material. An isotropic material needs only 2.

Isotropic materials

A tensile test gives \(\epsilon_{11} = \sigma_{11}/E\) and lateral contraction \(\epsilon_{22} = \epsilon_{33} = -\nu\epsilon_{11}\), with \(\nu\) the Poisson’s ratio. Superposing tests in three directions relates the diagonal components. A pure shear state (a square turning into a diamond) gives \(|\gamma| = |\tau|/G\) with the shear modulus

\[ G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \gamma_{12} = 2\epsilon_{12} = \frac{2(1+\nu)}{E}\sigma_{12}. \]

Collecting everything:

\[ \sigma_{ij} = \frac{E}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}\left[(1-2\nu)\,\epsilon_{ij} + \nu\sum_{k=1}^3\epsilon_{kk}\,\delta_{ij}\right], \qquad \epsilon_{ij} = \frac1E\left[(1+\nu)\,\sigma_{ij} - \nu\sum_{k=1}^3\sigma_{kk}\,\delta_{ij}\right]. \]

Slide example: using material properties

A steel bar with \(A = 25\,\text{mm}^2\), \(L = 10\,\text{cm}\), \(E = 200\,000\,\text{N/mm}^2\), \(\nu = 0.3\) is pulled with \(N = 5\,\text{kN}\). What is the elongation?

Plane stress and plane strain

Plane stress: a thin body loaded only in its plane, so \(\sigma_{13} = \sigma_{23} = \sigma_{33} = 0\). The thickness strain is generally nonzero:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{11}\\ \sigma_{22}\\ \sigma_{12}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{E}{1-\nu^2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & \nu & 0\\ \nu & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{1-\nu}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_{11}\\ \epsilon_{22}\\ 2\epsilon_{12}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \epsilon_{33} = -\frac{\nu}{E}(\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{22}). \]

Plane strain: a very long body loaded orthogonally to its length, so \(\epsilon_{13} = \epsilon_{23} = \epsilon_{33} = 0\). The out-of-plane stress is generally nonzero:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{11}\\ \sigma_{22}\\ \sigma_{12}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{E}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}\begin{bmatrix}1-\nu & \nu & 0\\ \nu & 1-\nu & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{1-2\nu}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_{11}\\ \epsilon_{22}\\ 2\epsilon_{12}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \sigma_{33} = \nu(\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{22}). \]

Lab: Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio

Pick a material or enter \(E\) and \(\nu\). The sketch shows a bar under uniaxial stress at strain \(\epsilon_{11}\) (exaggerated): it narrows by \(\nu\epsilon_{11}\). As \(\nu \to 0.5\) the volume stops changing; for negative \(\nu\) the bar gets wider.

Closing the loop

In each point of the body we solve for 15 unknowns: 3 displacements, 6 strains, 6 stresses. The 15 equations are 3 equilibrium equations, 6 kinematic equations and 6 constitutive equations, together with the boundary conditions

\[ q_i = \sum_{j=1}^3\sigma_{ji}n_j \;\text{ on } a_q, \qquad u_i = \bar u_i \;\text{ on } a_u. \]

This is the strong form of the problem; solving it gives the exact solution in every point. For complex problems that quickly becomes impractical, which motivates the energy principles of weeks 6 and 7.

6Week 6

Principle of virtual work

The lecture slides for this week aren’t uploaded yet. These notes follow the exercise sheet and will be updated when the slides are available.

Instead of writing equilibrium equations directly, we imagine a small virtual displacement \(\delta\mathbf u\) of the body and compare the work done by external and internal forces.

The principle

A body is in equilibrium if, for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement (one that respects the supports, \(\delta\mathbf u = \mathbf 0\) on \(a_u\)), the external virtual work equals the internal virtual work:

\[ \delta W_E = \delta W_I, \qquad \delta W_E = \int_v \rho f_i\,\delta u_i\,dv + \int_{a_q} q_i\,\delta u_i\,da, \qquad \delta W_I = \int_v \sigma_{ij}\,\delta\epsilon_{ij}\,dv. \]

It makes no assumption about the deformations, the loading or the material. For a mechanism of rigid bars the internal virtual work comes only from springs:

\[ \delta W_I = k(\ell - \ell_0)\,\delta\ell + \kappa(\phi - \phi_0)\,\delta\phi. \]

Recipe for mechanisms

  1. Describe the configuration with one angle (or a few) and write the positions of the loaded points.
  2. If several angles appear, find the geometric relation between them and differentiate it (for example \(5L\sin\beta = 3L\sin\gamma \Rightarrow 5L\cos\beta\,\delta\beta = 3L\cos\gamma\,\delta\gamma\)).
  3. Differentiate the positions to get the virtual displacements of the loaded points.
  4. Sum force times virtual displacement, set \(\delta W_E - \delta W_I = 0\), and divide by the arbitrary \(\delta\alpha\).

Lab: virtual work on the two-bar mechanism

The green bar pivots at the bottom, the top of the grey bar slides along the vertical. The lab finds the \(V\) that makes the total virtual work zero.

7Week 7

Minimum/stationary potential energy

The lecture slides for this week aren’t uploaded yet. These notes follow the exercise sheet and will be updated when the slides are available.

When the material is conservative (elastic) and the loads are conservative too, the virtual work can be written as the variation of a single function: the total potential energy.

Total potential

\[ \mathcal P = \mathcal U + \mathcal F, \qquad \mathcal U = \int_v u\,dv, \]

where \(\mathcal U\) is the elastic potential (stored strain energy) and \(\mathcal F\) the force potential, minus the work the loads do from the reference configuration. For the springs and loads in the exercises:

\[ \mathcal U_{\text{spring}} = \tfrac12 k(\ell - \ell_0)^2, \qquad \mathcal U_{\text{torsion}} = \tfrac12\kappa(\phi - \phi_0)^2, \qquad \mathcal F_{\text{gravity}} = mg\,\Delta(\text{height}), \qquad \mathcal F_{\text{force}} = -F\,\Delta(\text{position along } F). \]

Equilibrium and stability

Equilibrium configurations make the potential stationary; an equilibrium is stable if the potential is a minimum there:

\[ \frac{d\mathcal P}{d\theta} = 0 \;\;\text{(equilibrium)}, \qquad \frac{d^2\mathcal P}{d\theta^2} > 0 \;\;\text{(stable)}. \]

The critical load (or height, or stiffness) is where \(d^2\mathcal P/d\theta^2\) at the equilibrium passes through zero.

Unlike the principle of virtual work, minimum potential energy requires conservative materials. A permanently deformed sheet in deep drawing is a case for virtual work only.

Lab: stability of the inverted pendulum

Week 7, Exercise 4: a mass \(m\) at height \(h\) on a massless bar, held upright by a torsion spring \(k\). The total potential is \(\mathcal P(\theta) = \tfrac12k\theta^2 + mgh(\cos\theta - 1)\). Raise \(h\) past \(h_{\text{crit}} = k/(mg)\) and watch the minimum at \(\theta = 0\) turn into a maximum while two new stable equilibria appear.

8Week 8

Rayleigh–Ritz method and finite element method

The lecture slides for this week aren’t uploaded yet. These notes follow the exercise sheet and will be updated when the slides are available.

Solving the strong form exactly is rarely practical. The Rayleigh–Ritz method builds an approximate displacement field from the principle of minimum potential energy: guess the shape of the solution with a few unknown coefficients, and let the potential energy pick the best coefficients.

Total potential of a bar

For a bar with axial stiffness \(EA[x]\), a distributed load \(f[x]\) and a point load \(F\) at \(x = L\):

\[ \mathcal P = \underbrace{\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA[x]\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 dx}_{\mathcal U} \;\underbrace{-\int_0^L f[x]\,u[x]\,dx - F\,u[L]}_{\mathcal F}. \]

Supports add their own energy, for example \(\tfrac12 k A\,u[0]^2\) for a spring foundation of stiffness \(k\) per unit area. For a beam in bending the elastic part becomes \(\int_0^L \tfrac12 EI\,(v'')^2\,dx\).

The recipe

  1. Choose a trial displacement with degrees of freedom, e.g. \(u^{\text{trial}}[x] = ax + b\).
  2. Make it kinematically admissible: it must be continuous and satisfy the kinematic boundary conditions (e.g. \(u[0] = 0\) at a fixed end; \(v[0] = 0\) and \(v'[0] = 0\) at a clamped beam end). This usually removes some degrees of freedom.
  3. Substitute into \(\mathcal P\) and integrate.
  4. Make \(\mathcal P\) stationary: \(\partial\mathcal P/\partial a_i = 0\) for every remaining degree of freedom, and solve.
  5. Evaluate the approximation where asked, and judge its quality.

How good is the approximation?

  • If the exact solution can be written with the trial function, Rayleigh–Ritz finds it exactly. A linearly increasing load gives a cubic exact displacement, so a cubic trial is exact.
  • Adding a higher-order term while keeping all admissible lower-order terms can only improve the result. Dropping a lower-order term (e.g. using \(\beta x^2\) instead of \(\alpha x + \beta x^2\)) need not improve it.
  • The approximation is too stiff: displacements come out smaller than the exact ones. The tip of a cantilever with a quadratic trial deflects \(f_0L^3/(4EI)\) instead of the exact \(f_0L^3/(3EI)\).

Finite element method

Instead of one trial function for the whole body, the body is divided into elements. The unknowns are the nodal displacements, and inside each element the displacement is interpolated with shape functions:

\[ \mathbf u^{(e)}[\mathbf x] = \sum_{i} N_i[\mathbf x]\,\mathbf u_i, \qquad \#\text{DOF} = (\text{number of nodes}) \times (\text{dimensions}). \]

A four-node element in 3D has \(4 \times 3 = 12\) DOF; a three-node triangle in 2D has 6. To represent a curved geometry better, either use higher-order elements (extra mid-side nodes, so edges can curve) or more elements (a finer mesh follows the curve more closely).

A bar fixed at \(x = 0\), with \(EA = 1\), \(L = 1\). Pick the load and the trial function; the lab makes the trial kinematically admissible, minimises \(\mathcal P\) and compares with the exact solution. Try the cubic trial with the linear load: it lands exactly on the exact curve.

Exercises

Every exercise from the weekly sheets, many with an interactive figure. Type your answer and check it; you can enter numbers, fractions or expressions such as 1-a, sqrt(3)/2*(sqrt(3)+a) or (5a^2-1)/2. The live values under each figure are blurred until you choose to show them.

1Week 1 · notes

Strain measures

Watch out

  • A strain measure must be dimensionless and must vanish when nothing deforms.
  • Capitals \(X\) belong to the undeformed configuration, small \(x\) to the deformed one. The displacement is \(\mathbf u = \mathbf x - \mathbf X\).
  • In \(E_{ij}\) the quadratic term sums over \(k\): three products, not one. Write out all nine \(\partial u_k/\partial X_i\) first.
  • Differentiate first, then substitute the coordinates of the point.

Exercise 1What makes a strain measure?

A bar of length \(L\) deforms to length \(k\). Which formulas could serve as a strain measure?

Select every valid strain measure.

Worked solution

(a) equals 1 when \(k = L\), so it doesn’t vanish. (b) and (c) are dimensionless and vanish at \(k = L\). (d) has units of 1/length.

Exercise 2Mapping the corners of a block

A block of side \(L\) with corners \(A, B, C, D\) deforms by \(x = X + aY\), \(y = Y + X^2/L + bL\), with \(a, b \ge 0\). The displacement \(u_X\) is zero everywhere and \(y_c = \tfrac52L\). Tune \(a\) and \(b\) to match.

Worked solution

\(u_X = aY = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0\). At \(C\): \(y_c = L + L + bL = \tfrac52L \Rightarrow b = \tfrac12\). At \(P\): \(u_X = 0\), \(u_Y = \tfrac{L}{4} + \tfrac L2 = \tfrac34L\).

Exercise 3Choosing the deformed configuration

A block of side \(L\) undergoes the placement \(x = X + 0.5L\), \(y = Y + 0.5X\). Generalise it to \(x = X + tL\), \(y = Y + sX\) and use the sliders to see what each term does.

Tip The translation \(tL\) moves every point equally, so it never contributes to the strain.

E_XX
E_YY
E_XY

a) Which candidate is a valid deformed configuration for \(t = s = 0.5\)?

Worked solution

The translation \(tL\) moves every point equally; \(u_Y = sX\) shifts points upward in proportion to \(X\), turning the square into a parallelogram with vertical sides: configuration a). With \(\partial u_Y/\partial X = s\) the only nonzero gradient,

\[ E_{XY} = \tfrac12\left(0 + s\right) + \tfrac12\left(0\cdot 0 + s\cdot 0\right) = \tfrac s2 = \tfrac14. \]

Exercise 4A bar moved by four constants

A bar of length \(L\) undergoes \(x_1 = X_1 + (1 - \tfrac{X_1}{L})a + \tfrac{X_1}{L}b\), \(x_2 = X_2 + (1 - \tfrac{X_1}{L})c + \tfrac{X_1}{L}d\), \(x_3 = X_3\). The left end moves by \((a, c)\) and the right end by \((b, d)\).

E₁₁
E₁₂

Worked solution

\(u_1 = (1 - \tfrac{X_1}{L})a + \tfrac{X_1}{L}b\), \(u_2 = (1 - \tfrac{X_1}{L})c + \tfrac{X_1}{L}d\), \(u_3 = 0\).

\[ E_{11} = \frac{b-a}{L} + \frac12\left(\frac{b-a}{L}\right)^2 + \frac12\left(\frac{d-c}{L}\right)^2, \qquad E_{12} = \frac12\,\frac{d-c}{L}, \qquad \text{all others } 0. \]

Exercise 5Green–Lagrange components at a point

A body has \(u_1 = a\tfrac{X_1^2}{L} + b\tfrac{X_2^2}{L}\), \(u_2 = 3b\tfrac{X_1^2}{L} + c\tfrac{X_3^2}{L}\), \(u_3 = aX_3\), with no further assumptions. Evaluate at \(P = [L\;\; L\;\; 2L]\).

Worked solution
\[ E_{33} = a + 2c^2\frac{X_3^2}{L^2} + \frac12a^2, \quad E_{32} = c\frac{X_3}{L}, \quad E_{12} = b\frac{X_2}{L} + 3b\frac{X_1}{L} + 2ab\frac{X_1X_2}{L^2}. \]

At \(P\): \(a + 8c^2 + \tfrac12a^2\), \(2c\) and \(4b + 2ab\). Of 6 independent components, 3 remain.

Exercise 6Finding a from a known strain

A body deforms as \(u_X = a\tfrac{X^2}{L} + Y + 2Z\), \(u_Y = \tfrac{Z^2}{L} + 4Y\), \(u_Z = Z\), with \(a > 0\). At \(P\) located at \(\mathbf X_P^{\mathsf T} = [L\;\; 3L\;\; L]\), \(E_{XX} = 12\). Slide \(a\) until \(E_{XX}\) hits 12.

E_XX at P

Worked solution
\[ E_{XX} = \frac{\partial u_X}{\partial X} + \frac12\left(\frac{\partial u_X}{\partial X}\right)^2 = 2a + 2a^2 = 12 \;\Rightarrow\; a^2 + a - 6 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 2. \]
\[ E_{YY} = 4 + \tfrac12\left(1^2 + 4^2 + 0\right) = \tfrac{25}{2}, \qquad E_{XZ} = \tfrac12(2 + 0) + \tfrac12(4\cdot 2 + 0 + 0) = 5. \]
2Week 2 · notes

Strain tensors

Watch out

  • Normalise \(\mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf N\) before computing \(\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\mathbf M\).
  • The change in angle is \(\gamma_{12} = 2\epsilon_{12}\): keep the \(\tfrac12\) in \(\epsilon_{ij}\) and don’t lose the 2 in \(\gamma\).
  • Infinitesimal strain fails for large rotations too, not only for large deformations.
  • Check the axes in the figure: some sheets draw \(\mathbf e_2\) pointing down, which flips the sign of angles.

Exercise 1When is strain infinitesimal?

Assume continuum theory applies to all three situations: someone sitting on a chair, a pool ball being struck, and a car crashing into a tree.

For which situations can infinitesimal strain be assumed?

Worked solution

Only the chair: no large deformations and no large rotations. The pool ball rolls (large rotations) and the car crumples (large deformations).

Exercise 2Green–Lagrange versus Cauchy along a bar

A body deforms with \(u_1 = aX_1^2/L\), \(u_2 = u_3 = 0\), where \(a\) is dimensionless. Compare \(E_{11}\) with \(\epsilon_{11}\) along the body and see when they agree.

E₁₁ε₁₁

Worked solution

\(E_{11} = 2a\tfrac{X_1}{L} + 2a^2\tfrac{X_1^2}{L^2}\), \(E_{12} = E_{22} = 0\); \(\epsilon_{11} = 2a\tfrac{X_1}{L}\). Infinitesimal strain holds when \(2a^2\tfrac{X_1^2}{L^2} \ll 2a\tfrac{X_1}{L}\), i.e. when \(aX_1/L \ll 1\).

Exercise 3Strain along carbon fibres

An epoxy plate reinforced by carbon fibres has \(\boldsymbol\epsilon = \begin{bmatrix}2 & a & 3\\ a & 0 & 1\\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), with the fibres in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1\) and \(\mathbf e_2\) at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf e_1\). The strain along the fibres is \(\epsilon_m = \mathbf m^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\epsilon\,\mathbf m\) with \(\mathbf m = [\cos\theta\;\; \sin\theta\;\; 0]^{\mathsf T}\).

ε_m

Worked solution
\[ \epsilon_m = 2\cos^2\theta + 2a\cos\theta\sin\theta. \]

At \(135^\circ\): \(2\cdot\tfrac12 + 2a\cdot(-\tfrac12) = 1 - a\). At \(30^\circ\): \(2\cdot\tfrac34 + 2a\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}(\sqrt3 + a)\). At \(45^\circ\): \(1 + a = 3\), so \(a = 2\).

Exercise 4Three strain gauges

Three gauges at \(P = [\tfrac L2\;\; \tfrac L3\;\; L]\) read \(\epsilon_1 = 4a\) (along \(\mathbf e_2\)), \(\epsilon_2 = 3a\) (along \(\mathbf e_1\)) and \(\epsilon_3 = 2a\) (at \(45^\circ\) between them). Infinitesimal strain applies.

Worked solution

The gauges give \(\epsilon_{11} = 3a\), \(\epsilon_{22} = 4a\) and \(\tfrac12(\epsilon_{11} + \epsilon_{22}) + \epsilon_{12} = 2a\), so \(\epsilon_{12} = -\tfrac32a\). From \(u_1\): \(\epsilon_{11} = \tfrac{4X_1}{L} + \tfrac{3X_2}{L} = 2 + 1 = 3 = 3a\), so \(a = 1\).

Exercise 5Validating displacements with a gauge

A gauge along \(\mathbf e_z\) at \(P = [2L\;\; \tfrac L{16}\;\; \tfrac L{60}]\) reads \(\epsilon = 4\). The proposed displacements are \(u_x = 2\tfrac{y^2}{L} + 3\tfrac{z^2}{L}\), \(u_y = x + 4\tfrac{y^2}{L}\), \(u_z = 3z\).

Tip Off-diagonal components carry a factor \(\tfrac12\); the change in angle is twice the component.

⚠ Possible mistake in the official solution

The answers here follow the solution sheet: \(\epsilon_{xy} = \tfrac54\), \(\epsilon_{zx} = \tfrac1{10}\), \(\gamma_{zx} = \tfrac15\). Using the lecture definition \(\epsilon_{ij} = \tfrac12\left(\tfrac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} + \tfrac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right)\), the shear components come out half as large: \(\epsilon_{xy} = \tfrac58\), \(\epsilon_{zx} = \tfrac1{20}\), \(\gamma_{zx} = \tfrac1{10}\). Ask your instructor which is right before relying on it.

Worked solution

\(\epsilon_{xx} = 0\), \(\epsilon_{yy} = \tfrac12\), \(\epsilon_{zz} = 3\), \(\epsilon_{yz} = 0\), \(\epsilon_{xy} = \tfrac54\), \(\epsilon_{zx} = \tfrac1{10}\), so \(\gamma_{zx} = \tfrac15\) (values from the solution sheet). The gauge reads 4 while \(\epsilon_{zz} = 3\), so the displacements are wrong; \(u_z = 4z\) would match. One gauge can’t check the other directions.

Exercise 6Angle between two segments

A block of width \(\tfrac23L\) and height \(L\) undergoes \(x = aX + aY\), \(y = 2aY\). \(D\) lies at the middle of the bottom edge; \(A\) and \(B\) are the top corners. Find the Green–Lagrange strain tensor and the cosine of the angle between the deformed segments \(DA\) and \(DB\).

E₁₁
E₂₂
E₁₂
cos φ (deformed)
φ

Notice that the angle doesn’t change with \(a\). Why?

Worked solution
\[ E_{11} = \tfrac12(a^2 - 1), \quad E_{22} = \tfrac12(5a^2 - 1), \quad E_{12} = \tfrac12a^2. \]

The deformed segments are \(a\,(\tfrac23, 2)L\) and \(a\,(\tfrac43, 2)L\). The factor \(a\) cancels:

\[ \cos\varphi = \frac{\tfrac89 + 4}{\sqrt{\tfrac49 + 4}\,\sqrt{\tfrac{16}9 + 4}} = \frac{44}{\sqrt{2080}} = \frac{11}{\sqrt{130}}. \]

The same result follows from \(\cos\varphi = (\cos\Phi + 2\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\mathbf N)/(\sqrt{1+2E_M}\sqrt{1+2E_N})\).

3Week 3 · notes

Stress measures

Watch out

  • \(\mathbf p = \boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n\) needs a unit outward normal. “Parallel to \([1\;2]\)” still has to be normalised.
  • Opposite facets have opposite normals, so their stress vectors are opposite.
  • \(\sigma\) is a scalar, \(\boldsymbol\sigma_n = \sigma\mathbf n\) a vector. Read which one is asked.
  • Check principal stresses: they sum to \(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\sigma\). A decoupled row and column gives a principal value directly.

Exercise 1A facet in a uniform plane stress

At \(P\), \(\boldsymbol\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(5a, 5a, 0)\). The facet in the figure has outward normal \(\mathbf n = \tfrac1{\sqrt5}[1\;\; 2\;\; 0]^{\mathsf T}\).

d) What does this say about \(\mathbf n\)?

Worked solution

\(\mathbf p = 5a\,\mathbf n = \sqrt5a\,[1\;2\;0]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\sigma = 5a\), \(\tau = 0\): \(\mathbf n\) is a principal direction.

Exercise 2Rebuilding the stress tensor from stress vectors

At \(O\): \(\mathbf p_1 = [2a\;\; a\;\; 3a]^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\mathbf p_3 = [3a\;\; 2a\;\; 5a]^{\mathsf T}\). On a facet with \(\mathbf n_4 = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}[0\;1\;1]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mathbf p_4 = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}[4a\;\; 5a\;\; 7a]^{\mathsf T}\).

a) Do \(\mathbf p_1\) and \(\mathbf p_3\) alone fix \(\boldsymbol\sigma\)?

Worked solution

\(\mathbf p_2 = \sqrt2\mathbf p_4 - \mathbf p_3 = a[1\;3\;2]^{\mathsf T}\), so

\[ \boldsymbol\sigma = a\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3\\ 1 & 3 & 2\\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf p_5 = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathbf p_1 + \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\mathbf p_2 + 0\,\mathbf p_3 = \tfrac{a}{\sqrt2}[3\;4\;5]^{\mathsf T}. \]

Exercise 3Reinforced concrete

Steel bars lie at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) to \(\mathbf e_1\) in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1\) and \(\mathbf e_2\). At \(P\): \(\boldsymbol\sigma = s\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 1\\ 6 & 3 & 2\\ 1 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon = \begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 & 2\\ 1 & 3 & 2\\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\).

Worked solution

\(\mathbf p = \tfrac{s}{\sqrt2}[8\;9\;3]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\sigma = \tfrac{17}{2}s\), \(\boldsymbol\sigma_n = \tfrac{17\sqrt2}{4}s\,[1\;1\;0]^{\mathsf T}\). \(\epsilon_n = 3 + 1 + \tfrac32 = \tfrac{11}2\).

Exercise 4Match the stress vector

A 2D body has \(\boldsymbol\sigma(\mathbf x) = s\begin{bmatrix}2bx & axy\\ axy & 3ay^2\end{bmatrix}\). At \(Q\) located at \([L\;\; L]\), on a facet with outward normal parallel to \([2\;\; 0]\), the stress vector is \(s\,[2\;\; 5]^{\mathsf T}\). Tune \(aL^2\) and \(bL\) until your stress vector (red) lands on the target (dashed).

Tip The normal is parallel to \([2\;\;0]\): normalise it to \(\mathbf e_1\) before using it.

Worked solution
\[ \mathbf p_P = \frac{s}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}2bL + 2aL^2\\ aL^2 + 6aL^2\end{bmatrix} = \frac{s}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}2aL^2 + 2bL\\ 7aL^2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf p_Q = s\begin{bmatrix}2bL\\ aL^2\end{bmatrix} = s\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 5\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow a = \frac{5}{L^2},\; b = \frac1L. \]

Exercise 5Hunting for principal directions

At \(P\), \(\boldsymbol\sigma = c\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 2\\ 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\). Direction \(\mathbf e_2\) is decoupled, so it’s already principal with \(\sigma = 3c\). Rotate the facet normal in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1\) and \(\mathbf e_3\) and find the angles where the shear disappears.

σ / c
τ / c

Worked solution
\[ \det(\boldsymbol\sigma - \sigma\mathbf I) = (3c - \sigma)\left[(4c - \sigma)(c - \sigma) - 4c^2\right] = (3c - \sigma)\,\sigma\,(\sigma - 5c) = 0. \]

\(\sigma_1 = 0\) with \(\mathbf n_1 = \tfrac1{\sqrt5}[-1\;0\;2]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\sigma_2 = 3c\) with \(\mathbf n_2 = \mathbf e_2\), \(\sigma_3 = 5c\) with \(\mathbf n_3 = \tfrac1{\sqrt5}[2\;0\;1]^{\mathsf T}\), at \(\arctan\tfrac12 \approx 26.6^\circ\) from \(\mathbf e_1\).

Exercise 6Unknown constants from principal stresses

At \(Q\) on a \(45^\circ\) facet, \(\boldsymbol\sigma = q\begin{bmatrix}1 & \sqrt3b & 0\\ \sqrt3b & 3 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt2a\end{bmatrix}\). The principal stresses are \(0\), \(3\sqrt2q\) and \(4q\), and \(p_Y = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}(\sqrt3 - 1)q\).

Worked solution

The in-plane block gives \(\sigma = q\left(2 \pm \sqrt{1 + 3b^2}\right)\). Matching \(0\) and \(4q\) gives \(b = 1\) (the sign is fixed by \(p_Y\)); the remaining \(\sqrt2aq = 3\sqrt2q\) gives \(a = 3\).

4Week 4 · notes

Equilibrium equations

Watch out

  • Write the three terms of \(\sum_j \partial\sigma_{ji}/\partial x_j\) explicitly; each differentiates with respect to a different coordinate.
  • Mind the sign: \(\rho f_i = -\sum_j \partial\sigma_{ji}/\partial x_j\).
  • Boundary conditions hold on the loaded surface with its outward normal. A free surface has \(\mathbf q = \mathbf 0\).
  • A stress vector given on a facet with normal \(\mathbf e_y\) is a row of \(\boldsymbol\sigma\): use symmetry to get the column you need.

Exercise 1A bar in tension

A bar carries \(\mathbf q = -a\mathbf e_1\) on \(x_1 = 0\), \(\mathbf q = a\mathbf e_1\) on \(x_1 = L\), nothing elsewhere, and no body forces. Candidate: \(\boldsymbol\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(a, 0, 0)\). A plane \(\Pi\) cuts the bar at \(45^\circ\).

a) Does the candidate satisfy equilibrium in the volume and at the outer surface?

Worked solution

Volume: \(0 + 0 + 0 + \rho\cdot 0 = 0\) in each direction. Surfaces: \(\boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}[-1\;0\;0]^{\mathsf T} = [-a\;0\;0]^{\mathsf T}\), and so on. On \(\Pi\): \(\mathbf p = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}a\,\mathbf e_1\).

Exercise 2Force per unit mass from a stress vector

The stress vector on a facet with outward normal \(\mathbf e_y\) is \(\mathbf p_y^{\mathsf T} = \rho\,[2ax\;\; 4bxy\;\; 3ay + az]\). Using symmetry of \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) and equilibrium along \(\mathbf e_y\), find \(f_y\) at \(Q = [3L\;\; L\;\; 5L]\).

Worked solution
\[ \rho f_y = -\left(\frac{\partial(2\rho ax)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(4\rho bxy)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(\rho(3ay + az))}{\partial z}\right) = -\rho(3a + 4bx) \;\Rightarrow\; f_y\big|_Q = -3(a + 4bL). \]

Exercise 3Rotation and symmetry

Write the equilibrium in rotation of a small block about an axis parallel to \(\mathbf e_3\) through its centre.

b) Repeating for the other two axes shows that \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) is…

Worked solution

Moments of the shear forces give \(\left[(2\sigma_{12} + d\sigma_{12}) - (2\sigma_{21} + d\sigma_{21})\right]\tfrac12dx_1dx_2dx_3 = 0\), so \(\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21}\) and likewise for the other pairs.

Exercise 4A part with a groove

A grooved part is pulled with \(\mathbf q = -q\mathbf e_1\) on its left face and \(\mathbf q = q\mathbf e_1\) on its right face. Face \(A\) (blue) is a free face with normal \(\mathbf e_3\); face \(B\) (red) is a loaded face.

a) Which stress components vanish on face \(A\)?

c) Where do the highest stresses occur?

Worked solution

Face \(A\): \(\sigma_{31} = \sigma_{32} = \sigma_{33} = 0\). Face \(B\): \(\sigma_{11} = q\), \(\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{13} = 0\).

Exercise 5The body force that keeps a body in equilibrium

A body carries \(\boldsymbol\sigma = \rho a\begin{bmatrix}x^2 & xy & z^2\\ xy & x^2 & 0\\ z^2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\). Equilibrium in the volume requires \(\rho f_i = -\sum_j \partial\sigma_{ji}/\partial x_j\). The arrows show that required force per unit volume in a slice at height \(z\).

Hover or tap the field to read \(\rho\mathbf f\) at a point.

Worked solution

At \(P\) every component vanishes, so \(\mathbf p = \mathbf 0\). At \(Q\) the principal stresses are \(-\rho aL^2\), \(0\) and \(3\rho aL^2\). In the volume:

\[ \rho\mathbf f = -\rho a\begin{bmatrix}2x + x + 2z\\ y + 0 + 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix} = -\rho a\begin{bmatrix}3x + 2z\\ y\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. \]

Exercise 6Locating a point from equilibrium

\(\boldsymbol\sigma = \rho f\begin{bmatrix}bx^2 & ay & bxz\\ ay & cxy^2 & 0\\ bxz & 0 & cyz^2\end{bmatrix}\) with unknown \(a, b, c\). At \(Q = [\tfrac L2\;\; -\tfrac L4\;\; \tfrac L2]\) on the top surface (normal at \(45^\circ\)), \(\mathbf q_Q = \rho f\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}[L\;\; -\tfrac L8\;\; \tfrac L8]^{\mathsf T}\). At \(P\) with \(z_P = 0\), \(\mathbf f_P = f[-2\;\; -3\;\; 0]^{\mathsf T}\).

Tip The slanted top surface has normal \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}[1\;0\;1]^{\mathsf T}\). Find \(a, b, c\) from \(Q\) before looking at \(P\).

Worked solution

At \(Q\): \(\tfrac{bL^2}{2} = L \Rightarrow b = \tfrac2L\); \(-\tfrac{aL}4 = -\tfrac L8 \Rightarrow a = \tfrac12\); \(\tfrac L2 - \tfrac{cL^3}{16} = \tfrac L8 \Rightarrow c = \tfrac6{L^2}\).

In the volume, \(\rho\mathbf f = -\rho f\,[3bx + a\;\; 2cxy\;\; bz + 2cyz]^{\mathsf T}\). At \(P\): \(\tfrac{6x}{L} + \tfrac12 = 2 \Rightarrow x_P = \tfrac L4\), and \(\tfrac{12xy}{L^2} = 3 \Rightarrow y_P = L\).

5Week 5 · notes

Constitutive equations

Watch out

  • Plane stress: \(\sigma_{33} = 0\) but \(\epsilon_{33} \neq 0\). Plane strain: \(\epsilon_{33} = 0\) but \(\sigma_{33} \neq 0\).
  • The matrix form uses \(2\epsilon_{12}\), and the strain energy has \(2\sigma_{12}\epsilon_{12}\). Don’t drop the 2.
  • Volume change: the linear estimate is \(\epsilon_{11} + \epsilon_{22} + \epsilon_{33}\); the exact one is \((1+\epsilon_{11})(1+\epsilon_{22})(1+\epsilon_{33}) - 1\). Check which one is expected.
  • Give answers in the constants of the problem (\(a\), \(p\), \(E\)) and check the units.

Exercise 1A small quadrilateral in plane stress

Quadrilateral \(ABCD\) has a \(60^\circ\) angle at \(A\). \(\|\mathbf p_{AB}\| = \|\mathbf p_{CD}\| = a\), aligned with face \(AD\); \(\|\mathbf p_{AD}\| = \|\mathbf p_{BC}\| = 2a\), aligned with face \(AB\). Type \(\nu\) as v.

Worked solution
\[ \boldsymbol\sigma = \frac a2\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt3 & -1\\ -1 & \sqrt3\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \epsilon_{AB} = \frac{\sqrt3a}{2E}(3 - \nu), \qquad \epsilon_{AD} = \frac{\sqrt3a}{E}(1 - \nu). \]

Exercise 2A block in a notch

A thin block (plane stress) of length \(L\) and height \(H\) sits in a rigid notch of length \(\ell = 1.003L\). A pressure \(p\) on top squeezes it to \(h = 0.99H\), and at that moment its sides just touch the notch. Find \(\nu\) and \(E\). Deformations are drawn 20× larger.

Worked solution
\[ \epsilon_{22} = \frac{h - H}{H} = -0.01 = -\frac pE \Rightarrow E = 100p, \qquad \epsilon_{11} = \frac{\ell - L}{L} = 0.003 = -\nu\,\epsilon_{22} \Rightarrow \nu = 0.3. \]

Exercise 3Deforming a square plate

A square plate (side \(L\), thickness \(T\), plane stress) has \(E = 30a\), \(\nu = 0.2\) and \(\boldsymbol\sigma = \begin{bmatrix}10a & -5a\\ -5a & 20a\end{bmatrix}\). Drag the slider to apply the stress gradually and watch the plate deform.

Tip The sheet’s volume change uses the exact product of stretches, not the linear sum of strains.

ε₁₁
ε₂₂
ε₃₃
γ₁₂

Worked solution
\[ \epsilon_{11} = \frac{10 - 0.2\cdot 20}{30} = 0.2, \quad \epsilon_{22} = \frac{20 - 0.2\cdot 10}{30} = 0.6, \quad \epsilon_{12} = \frac{1.2\cdot(-5)}{30} = -0.2, \quad \epsilon_{33} = -\frac{0.2\cdot 30}{30} = -0.2. \]

\(\gamma_{12} = -\tfrac25\), \(\Delta T = -\tfrac15T\), \(\Delta V = (1.2\cdot 1.6\cdot 0.8 - 1)L^2T = \tfrac{67}{125}L^2T\), \(u = \tfrac12(10\cdot 0.2 + 20\cdot 0.6 + 2\cdot 5\cdot 0.2)a = 8a\).

Exercise 4A wooden plank

A wooden plank, thin along \(\mathbf e_3\), carries \(\mathbf f_1\) in its plane, \(\mathbf f_2\) along \(\mathbf e_1\) on its long side and \(\mathbf f_3\) along \(\mathbf e_3\) on its thin side.

Select the true statements.

Worked solution

Only (b): thin along \(\mathbf e_3\) and loaded in-plane by \(\mathbf f_1\). (a) fails because of \(\mathbf f_2\); wood is anisotropic, so (c) fails; \(\mathbf f_3\) acts out of plane, so (d) fails.

Exercise 5A long tunnel lining

A very long isotropic body along \(\mathbf e_1\) with constant cross-section is loaded orthogonally to its length and only deforms in the plane orthogonal to it. Type \(\nu\) as v.

a) Which assumption applies?

Worked solution

Plane strain. Removing the rows and columns for the long direction from Hooke’s tensor:

\[ \mathbf C^{-1} = \frac{1+\nu}{E}\begin{bmatrix}1-\nu & -\nu & 0\\ -\nu & 1-\nu & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad u = \frac{E\left[(1-\nu)(\epsilon_{a}^2 + \epsilon_{b}^2) + 2\nu\epsilon_a\epsilon_b + 2(1-2\nu)\epsilon_{ab}^2\right]}{2(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \]

and the stress along the length is \(\nu\) times the sum of the two in-plane normal stresses.

Exercise 6A cork

A cork deforms with \(\mathbf u = \left[2x + \tfrac{xy}{L} + \tfrac{x^2}{L}\;\;\; y + \tfrac{xyz}{L^2}\;\;\; \tfrac{z^2}{L}\right]^{\mathsf T}\), infinitesimal strain, \(E = 10\,\text{N/m}^2\), \(\nu = 0\), \(\rho = 150\,\text{kg/m}^3\). Evaluate at \(P = L[1\;1\;1]\).

Worked solution
\[ \boldsymbol\epsilon = \begin{bmatrix}2 + \frac{2x}L + \frac yL & \frac x{2L} + \frac{yz}{2L^2} & 0\\ \cdot & 1 + \frac{xz}{L^2} & \frac{xy}{2L^2}\\ \cdot & \cdot & \frac{2z}L\end{bmatrix}. \]

At \(P\): \(\epsilon_{xx} = 5\), \(\sigma_{zz} = 10\cdot 2 = 20\,\text{N/m}^2\). \(\rho f_z = -E\left(\tfrac{x}{2L^2} + \tfrac2L\right) = -\tfrac{25}{L}\), so \(f_z = -\tfrac{1}{6L}\).

6Week 6 · notes

Principle of virtual work

Watch out

  • Virtual displacements must be kinematically admissible: zero wherever the support blocks motion.
  • Work is force times the displacement of its own point, in the force’s direction. A force pointing left does positive work for a leftward \(\delta\).
  • With several angles, write the geometric constraint first and differentiate it.
  • Collect everything as \((\ldots)\,\delta\alpha = 0\) and only then drop \(\delta\alpha\).

Exercise 1The two-bar mechanism

Two bars of length \(L\): the green one is pinned at the bottom, the top of the grey one slides along \(\mathbf e_y\). Forces \(V\) and \(H\) act as shown. The virtual work lab in the notes animates this mechanism.

Worked solution

\(\delta h = L\cos\alpha\,\delta\alpha\), \(\delta v = 2L\sin\alpha\,\delta\alpha\); \(H\cos\alpha + 2V\sin\alpha = 0\), so \(V/H = -\tfrac12\) at \(45^\circ\). A free-body diagram gives the same.

Exercise 2When does virtual work apply?

Which deformations can be studied with the principle of virtual work?

Worked solution

All four: the principle makes no assumption about the deformations, the loads or the materials.

Exercise 3Two bars with a sliding support

Two rigid bars of length \(5L\): the grey bar is pinned at the left; the green bar slides along \(\mathbf e_x\) at three fifths of its length. \(V\) acts at the joint, \(H\) at the right end. Raise \(\beta\) and watch \(\gamma\) follow from \(5L\sin\beta = 3L\sin\gamma\).

Tip Write \(5L\sin\beta = 3L\sin\gamma\) first; every virtual displacement then follows in terms of \(\delta\beta\).

γ
V / H for equilibrium

Worked solution

\(\delta v = 5L\cos\beta\,\delta\beta\) at the joint and \(\delta h = -5L\sin\beta\,\delta\beta - \tfrac{25}{3}L\tan\gamma\cos\beta\,\delta\beta\) at the end. Virtual work with \(V\) up and \(H\) pointing left:

\[ V\cos\beta + H\sin\beta + \tfrac53H\tan\gamma\cos\beta = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac VH = -\left(\tan\beta + \tfrac53\tan\gamma\right). \]

At \(\beta = 20^\circ\): \(\gamma \approx 34.76^\circ\), \(V/H \approx -1.52\).

Exercise 4A bar and a rigid triangle

A bar of length \(\sqrt2L\), pinned at point 1, carries a rigid triangle (sides \(L, L, \sqrt2L\)) whose top corner 4 slides along \(\mathbf e_y\). \(V\) acts at point 2, \(F\) at \(45^\circ\) at point 3. The bar turns by \(\theta\), the triangle by \(\varphi\).

a) Are \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) independent?

Worked solution

\(\delta y_2 = -\sqrt2L\sin\theta\,\delta\theta\), \(\delta x_3 = \sqrt2L\cos\theta\,\delta\theta - L\sin\varphi\,\delta\varphi\), \(\delta y_3 = -\sqrt2L\sin\theta\,\delta\theta - L\cos\varphi\,\delta\varphi\), with \(\delta\varphi = \tfrac{\sqrt2\cos\theta}{\sin\varphi + \cos\varphi}\delta\theta\).

\[ -\sqrt2V\sin\theta + F\left(\sin\theta + \frac{2\cos\theta\cos\varphi}{\sin\varphi + \cos\varphi}\right) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; V = \frac{3\sqrt2}{2}F \text{ at } 45^\circ. \]

Exercise 5A scissor mechanism with two springs

Five bars of length \(L\), a linear spring \(k\) (unstretched at \(\theta_0\)) and a torsion spring \(\kappa\) (unstretched at \(\phi_0\)), loaded by \(P\), \(W\), \(V\) and a moment \(M\).

Worked solution
\[ \delta W_I = \left[kL^2\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \sin\theta_0) + 4\kappa(\theta - \theta_0)\right]\delta\theta, \]
\[ M + PL\cos\theta - VL\sin\theta - WL\sin\theta - kL^2\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \sin\theta_0) - 4\kappa(\theta - \theta_0) = 0. \]

Fully collapsed (\(\theta = 0\)): \(M + PL + kL^2\sin\theta_0 + 4\kappa\theta_0 = 0\).

Exercise 6Displacements in a bar structure

Bars \(AB\), \(BC\), \(DC\) have stiffnesses \(2k_0\), \(k_0\), \(\tfrac43k_0\); bar \(EF\) is rigid with length \(2.5L\), hinged at \(F\). A load \(P\) acts at \(E\). The drawing exaggerates the displacements; slide \(P\) to load it.

u_B (P/k₀ = 1)
u_C
u_E

Worked solution
\[ \delta W_I = k_0(3u_B - u_C)\,\delta u_B + k_0(2u_C - u_B)\,\delta u_C, \qquad \delta W_E = \tfrac52P\,\delta u_C. \]

Both coefficients must match for arbitrary \(\delta u_B, \delta u_C\): \(u_C = 3u_B\) and \(5u_B = \tfrac52P/k_0\), so \(u_B = \tfrac{P}{2k_0}\), \(u_C = \tfrac{3P}{2k_0}\), \(u_C - u_B = \tfrac{P}{k_0}\).

7Week 7 · notes

Minimum potential energy

Watch out

  • Minimum potential energy needs conservative materials and loads; virtual work doesn’t.
  • Force potential is minus the work: \(\mathcal F = -F\,\Delta x\) along the force, \(mg\,\Delta h\) for gravity.
  • Torsion springs and angles in \(\mathcal P\) use radians.
  • Stability: evaluate \(d^2\mathcal P/d\theta^2\) at the equilibrium, after substituting the equilibrium load.

Exercise 1The mechanism with a spring

The week 6 mechanism with a spring \(k\), unloaded at \(\alpha_0 = 60^\circ\). Total potential: \(\mathcal P = 2kL^2(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0)^2 + HL(\sin\alpha - \sin\alpha_0) - 2VL(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0)\). The plot uses \(L = 1\).

Green dots: stable equilibria. Red: unstable.

⚠ Possible mistake in the official solution

The answer here follows the solution sheet: \(-4kL(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0) + H\cos\alpha + 2V\sin\alpha = 0\). Differentiating \(\mathcal U = 2kL^2(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0)^2\) gives an extra factor \(\sin\alpha\) on the spring term: \(-4kL\sin\alpha(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0) + H\cos\alpha + 2V\sin\alpha = 0\). The sheet’s stability condition \(k > \tfrac{H}{2L} - \tfrac VL\) only follows with that factor. Ask your instructor before relying on it.

Worked solution

\(\mathcal U = 2kL^2(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0)^2\), \(\mathcal F = HL(\sin\alpha - \sin\alpha_0) - 2VL(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0)\). The solution sheet gives the equilibrium equation \(-4kL(\cos\alpha - \cos\alpha_0) + H\cos\alpha + 2V\sin\alpha = 0\); the second derivative at \(\alpha = 45^\circ\), \(\alpha_0 = 60^\circ\) is positive if \(k > \tfrac{H}{2L} - \tfrac VL\).

Exercise 2Deep drawing

A thin metal sheet is deep-drawn. The figure shows its deformed shape and a proposed virtual displacement.

Select the true statements.

Worked solution

(a) true: virtual work makes no material assumptions. (b) false: minimum potential energy needs conservative materials. (c) false: the left support condition is violated. (d) true.

Exercise 3Buckling of a spring-supported pair of bars

Two rigid bars of length \(L\), pinned together and held horizontal by a spring of stiffness \(c\) at the middle hinge. A force \(F\) pushes on the roller at the right. The total potential is \(\mathcal P = \tfrac12cL^2\sin^2\alpha + 2FL(\cos\alpha - 1)\). Increase \(F\) until \(\alpha = 0\) stops being a minimum.

Tip Check stability at \(\alpha = 0\) itself: the curvature there changes sign at \(F_{\text{crit}}\).

Mechanism at the selected α

𝒫(α) / (cL²)

Worked solution
\[ \frac{d\mathcal P}{d\alpha} = \sin\alpha\,(cL^2\cos\alpha - 2FL) = 0 \Rightarrow F = \frac{cL}{2}\cos\alpha, \qquad \frac{d^2\mathcal P}{d\alpha^2}\Big|_{0} = cL^2 - 2FL > 0 \iff F < \frac{cL}{2}. \]

Exercise 4The inverted pendulum

Mass \(m\) at height \(h\), torsion spring \(k\) unloaded at \(\theta = 0\). The stability lab in the notes plots \(\mathcal P(\theta)\) for this system.

Worked solution

\(\mathcal U = \tfrac12k\theta^2\), \(\mathcal F = mgh(\cos\theta - 1)\); \(k\theta - mgh\sin\theta = 0\) gives \(m = \tfrac{k\theta}{gh\sin\theta} \approx 1.07\,\text{kg}\) at \(30^\circ\); \(h_{\text{crit}} = \tfrac{k}{mg}\).

Exercise 5A mechanism with a torsion spring and a hanging mass

A long bar \(L\) pinned at the left and a short bar \(L/2\) sliding along \(\mathbf e_x\), joined by a torsion spring \(\kappa\) (unloaded at \(\gamma_0\)). Force \(F\) at the slider, mass \(m\) hanging from the end of the long bar. Type \(\beta\) as b.

Worked solution

\(\mathcal U = \tfrac12\kappa(\gamma - \gamma_0)^2\), \(\mathcal F = FL(\cos\beta - \cos\beta_0) + mgL(\sin\beta - \sin\beta_0)\), \(\gamma = \pi - 2\beta\).

\[ F = \frac{4\kappa}{L}\,\frac{\beta - \beta_0}{\sin\beta} + mg\,\frac{\cos\beta}{\sin\beta}. \]

Exercise 6Car suspension

Two rigid bars of length \(a\), a vertical distance \(b\) apart, carry the wheel’s T-piece. A diagonal spring \(k\) is unloaded at \(\varphi_0 = 0\). Its length is \(\ell = \sqrt{a^2 - 2ab\sin\varphi + b^2}\), and equilibrium requires \(F = kb\,(\ell_0/\ell - 1)\).

Linkage at the selected φ

F / (kb) against φ

ℓ₀ / a
ℓ / a
F / (kb)

Worked solution

With \(\mathcal P = \tfrac12k(\ell - \ell_0)^2 - Fa\sin\varphi\) and \(d\ell/d\varphi = -ab\cos\varphi/\ell\):

\[ \frac{d\mathcal P}{d\varphi} = -k(\ell - \ell_0)\frac{ab\cos\varphi}{\ell} - Fa\cos\varphi = 0 \Rightarrow F = kb\left(\frac{\ell_0}{\ell} - 1\right). \]

At \(20^\circ\) with \(a = b\): \(F/(kb) = \sqrt2/\sqrt{2 - 2\sin 20^\circ} - 1 \approx 0.233\).

Exercise 7Week 6 revisited

Solve the week 6 exercises with minimum potential energy instead of virtual work. For Exercise 1: \(H\) (pointing left) acts at horizontal position \(L\sin\alpha\), and \(V\) (pointing up) at height \(2L\cos\alpha\). Write the force potential and make it stationary.

Worked solution

\(d\mathcal F/d\alpha = HL\cos\alpha + 2VL\sin\alpha = 0\): the same equation as with virtual work, as expected for rigid bars and constant forces.

8Week 8 · notes

Rayleigh–Ritz and FEM

Watch out

  • Check both conditions for kinematic admissibility: continuity and every kinematic boundary condition (a clamped beam end needs \(v = 0\) and \(v' = 0\)).
  • Apply the boundary conditions before substituting into \(\mathcal P\); that removes degrees of freedom.
  • Mind the sign of the force potential: a load pointing along \(+x\) gives \(-\int f u\,dx\); a load against \(x\) gives \(+\).
  • Count DOF as nodes × dimensions, not nodes alone.

Exercise 1A bar with a sine trial

A bar (length \(L\), area \(A\), modulus \(E\)) is fixed at \(x = 0\) and loaded by a constant distributed load \(f\). Trial: \(u^{\text{trial}}[x] = a\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{2L}\). The Rayleigh–Ritz lab compares this trial with the exact solution.

a) Is the trial kinematically admissible as given?

Worked solution
\[ \mathcal P = \tfrac12EA\,a^2\frac{\pi^2}{4L^2}\cdot\frac L2 - fa\,\frac{2L}{\pi}, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal P}{\partial a} = 0 \Rightarrow a = \frac{16fL^2}{\pi^3EA}, \qquad u\!\left[\tfrac L2\right] = \frac{8\sqrt2\,fL^2}{\pi^3EA}. \]

Exercise 2A cantilever beam

A beam (length \(L\), \(EI\) constant) is clamped at \(x = 0\) and loaded at its tip by \(f_0\). Trial: \(v^{\text{trial}}[x] = ax^2 + bx + c\). The exact tip deflection of a cantilever with a tip load is \(PL^3/(3EI)\).

a) Which coefficients must vanish for kinematic admissibility?

Worked solution

\(v[0] = c = 0\) and \(v'[0] = b = 0\), so \(v = ax^2\). \(\mathcal P = 2EIa^2L - f_0aL^2\) gives \(a = \tfrac{f_0L}{4EI}\) and a tip deflection \(\tfrac{f_0L^3}{4EI}\): 25% too small, because a quadratic can’t represent the exact cubic. With \(v = ax^3 + bx^2\): \(a = -\tfrac{f_0}{6EI}\), \(b = \tfrac{f_0L}{2EI}\), and the tip deflection \(\tfrac{f_0L^3}{3EI}\) is exact.

Exercise 3A linearly increasing load

A bar fixed at \(x = 0\) carries \(f[x] = f_0\tfrac xL\). Trial: \(u^{\text{trial}}[x] = ax + b\).

Worked solution

Linear: \(a = \tfrac{f_0L}{3EA}\). It gets the tip right but is poor inside the bar; a linearly increasing load needs a cubic displacement. Cubic: \(a = -\tfrac{f_0}{6EAL}\), \(b = 0\), \(c = \tfrac{f_0L}{2EA}\), which is the exact solution: \(u[L/2] = \tfrac{11}{48}\tfrac{f_0L^2}{EA}\) versus \(\tfrac16\) with the linear trial.

Exercise 4A tower on soft ground

A tower (bar) of height \(L\) has \(A[x] = A_0(2 - \tfrac xL)\), carries a pressure \(f\) on top and rests on springs with stiffness \(k\) per unit area.

Worked solution
\[ \mathcal P = \tfrac12EA_0\!\int_0^L\!\left(2 - \tfrac xL\right)(u')^2dx + \tfrac12kA[0]\,u[0]^2 + fA[L]\,u[L]. \]

Constant: \(u = -\tfrac f{2k}\). Linear: \(\mathcal P = \tfrac34EA_0La^2 + kA_0c^2 + fA_0(aL + c)\), so \(u = -\tfrac{2f}{3E}x - \tfrac f{2k}\).

Exercise 5A four-node element in 3D

Worked solution
\[ \mathbf d^{(e)\mathsf T} = [u_{x1}\;u_{y1}\;u_{z1}\;u_{x2}\;\ldots\;u_{z4}], \qquad u^{(e)}_x[\mathbf x] = \sum_{i=1}^4 N_i[\mathbf x]\,u_{xi}, \]

and likewise for \(u_y^{(e)}\) and \(u_z^{(e)}\).

Exercise 6A curved shelf

A shelf with a curved bottom is modelled in 2D with one linear triangle (three nodes) under a parabolic load.

Worked solution

One linear triangle: \(2 \times 3 = 6\). Higher-order approximation: curved edges become possible, \(2 \times 6 = 12\). More elements: the mesh follows the curve more closely, \(2 \times 7 = 14\).

Exam questions

Every sub-question from the January and April exams of 2025 and 2026, sorted by the week whose material it tests. Statements are condensed; the figures are from the exams. Each card has answer checks where the answer is a value, and the model answer from the solution sheets.

FormatTwo questions of equal weight, each built from several sub-questions.
AllowedThe formula sheet. No calculator.
