Scope this yearSlides of weeks 1–5 and the exercise sheets up to week 8.

Start with the recurring question types
★Overview

Recurring question types

Across the four exams the same eleven question types keep coming back. Question 1 is usually built from types 1–6, question 2 from types 7–11. Open a type for a short recipe, the slip that costs the most points, and links to every place it appears.

1Choosing strain gauges and finding constants2 exams

Recognise it Displacements with unknown constants, a point, gauge readings and several gauge setups.

  1. Compute the strain components at the point from the displacements, in terms of the unknowns.
  2. Note which components are already known (independent of the unknowns).
  3. Each gauge gives one equation \(\epsilon_M = \mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\epsilon\,\mathbf M\). A good setup gives as many independent equations as there are unknown components; a gauge along an already-known component is wasted.
  4. Solve, then check the readings with the values found.

Common slip Forgetting to justify why the other setups fail. Say it per setup: “only one useful measure for two unknowns”.

Apr 2026 1aJan 2025 1cWeek 2 Ex. 4Week 2 Ex. 5

2Change in angle: finding constants from cos φ2 exams

Recognise it Two directions \(\mathbf M\), \(\mathbf N\), a given \(\cos\varphi\) after deformation, and an unknown in \(\mathbf E\) or in the placement.

  1. Write \(\cos\varphi = \dfrac{\cos\Phi + 2\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\mathbf N}{\sqrt{1+2E_M}\sqrt{1+2E_N}}\) (on the formula sheet).
  2. Normalise \(\mathbf M\), \(\mathbf N\) and read \(\Phi\) from the figure (often \(\pi/2\)).
  3. Compute \(2\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\mathbf N\), \(E_M\), \(E_N\) separately and number them, as the model answers do.
  4. Solve; with a quadratic, pick the root allowed by the given sign condition.

Common slip Using \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) instead of \(\mathbf E\) when no small-strain assumption is made.

Jan 2026 1aApr 2025 1aWeek 2 Ex. 6

3Stress vector on a cut or facet2 exams

Recognise it A body is cut, a point lies on the cut, and the normal stress or the shear (tangent) stress vector is asked or given.

  1. Find the outward unit normal of the part you study, from the geometry of the cut.
  2. \(\mathbf p = \boldsymbol\sigma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n\), evaluated at the point.
  3. \(\sigma = \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p\); \(\boldsymbol\sigma_\tau = \mathbf p - \sigma\mathbf n\), or \((\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf t)\mathbf t\) in 2D.
  4. Add the extra relation from the stress state (e.g. plane strain: \(\sigma_{33} = \nu(\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{22})\)).

Common slip Taking the normal of the wrong part: the left and right part have opposite normals.

Apr 2025 1bApr 2026 1bWeek 3 Ex. 1Week 3 Ex. 4

4Constants or body forces from volume equilibrium2 exams

Recognise it A stress field depending on position, and \(\rho\mathbf f\) or \(f_i\) at a point given or asked.

  1. Write \(\sum_j \partial\sigma_{ji}/\partial x_j + \rho f_i = 0\) for each needed direction, with all three terms written out.
  2. Differentiate first, then substitute the coordinates of the point.
  3. Solve one direction at a time; often one equation contains a single unknown.

Common slip Substituting the point before differentiating, or losing the sign of \(\rho f_i\).

Jan 2025 1bApr 2026 1bWeek 4 Ex. 2Week 4 Ex. 6

5Boundary conditions on a loaded edge2 exams

Recognise it A force per unit area on an edge or small face, and equilibrium equations or stresses at that edge asked.

  1. Outward unit normal of the edge from the geometry (angles and side lengths).
  2. Components of \(\mathbf q\) from its magnitude and direction; pressing into the body gives negative components along \(\mathbf n\).
  3. Write \(q_i = \sum_j\sigma_{ji}n_j\) for each in-plane direction.
  4. Add any extra given relation and solve.

Common slip Wrong sign of \(\mathbf q\). Draw the arrow and read off each component.

Jan 2025 1dJan 2026 1cWeek 4 Ex. 1Week 4 Ex. 4

6Plane stress, strong form and material behaviour3 exams

Recognise it “Which assumption allows a 2D model?”, “write the strong form”, “is this curve elastic?”.

  1. Name the assumption and give both reasons (thin in one direction; loaded only in the plane).
  2. List the unknowns: displacements, strains, stresses.
  3. Write kinematic, equilibrium and constitutive equations fully and separately.
  4. Finish with boundary conditions: static on \(a_q\) (with the outward normal), kinematic on \(a_u\).

Common slip Calling a nonlinear curve inelastic. Elastic means unloading retraces loading; linear is a separate property.

Jan 2025 1aJan 2026 1bApr 2025 1cApr 2025 1dWeek 5 Ex. 5

7Relating virtual angles: f[α, γ]3 exams

Recognise it A mechanism described by two angles, and “build \(f\) such that \(\delta\gamma = f\,\delta\alpha\)”.

  1. Find a distance that can’t change because of a support or slider (e.g. the height difference between two pinned points, or a horizontal position fixed by a vertical slider).
  2. Write that distance with both angles, along both branches of the mechanism.
  3. Take the variation and set it to zero.
  4. Solve for the ratio of virtual angles.

Common slip Mixing up which angle is measured from the horizontal and which from the vertical: sin and cos swap.

Jan 2025 2aJan 2026 2bApr 2026 2aWeek 6 Ex. 3Week 6 Ex. 4

8Virtual work for a mechanism3 exams

Recognise it “Use the principle of virtual work” with forces, masses and springs on a mechanism.

  1. Write the position of each loaded point along the direction of its force; take the variation.
  2. External: \(\delta W_E = \sum F\,\delta x\), with the sign set by the force direction.
  3. Internal (springs): \(\delta W_I = k\,\Delta\ell\,\delta\Delta\ell\), with \(\Delta\ell\) measured from the unloaded configuration.
  4. Express everything in one virtual angle using \(f\) (keep \(f\) symbolic if the question says so), then \(\delta W_E = \delta W_I\).

Common slip Replacing \(f\) by its expression when the question says to keep it, or using a different principle: full points require the one asked.

Jan 2025 2bJan 2026 2bApr 2026 2aWeek 6 Ex. 1Week 6 Ex. 5

9Force potentials and minimum potential energy3 exams

Recognise it “Compute the force potential”, “its variation”, or “use minimum potential energy to find \(k\) / \(M\)”.

  1. Gravity: \(\mathcal F = mg\,(h - h_0)\). Constant force: \(\mathcal F = -F\,(x - x_0)\) along its direction.
  2. Spring: \(\mathcal U = \tfrac12k(\ell - \ell_0)^2\), with \(\ell\) from the geometry (often via Pythagoras).
  3. \(\mathcal P = \mathcal U + \mathcal F\); set \(d\mathcal P/d\varphi = 0\) and solve.
  4. For stability, check \(d^2\mathcal P/d\varphi^2 > 0\) at the equilibrium.

Common slip Forgetting that \(\mathcal F\) is minus the work: a mass going down lowers \(\mathcal F\).

Jan 2026 2aJan 2025 2cApr 2026 2bWeek 7 Ex. 3Week 7 Ex. 5

10Assumptions behind the energy principles3 exams

Recognise it “Which assumption…?”, “what does it require?”, “compatible versus admissible?”, “draw the admissible displacements”.

  1. Kinematically admissible: continuity of the body and the kinematic boundary conditions; then reactions do no virtual work.
  2. Compatible only requires continuity.
  3. Minimum potential energy also needs a conservative material and conservative forces.
  4. Always apply the answer to the given mechanism: which joints can’t move, which slide, why the material and forces are conservative.

Common slip Giving only the general definition without saying what it means for the specific supports and loads.

Jan 2025 2dJan 2026 2cApr 2026 2cWeek 7 Ex. 2

11Rayleigh–Ritz approximation1 exam

Recognise it A trial displacement with unknown coefficients for a bar or beam.

  1. Make it admissible: continuity and kinematic boundary conditions; this removes coefficients.
  2. Write \(\mathcal P\): elastic part \(\int\tfrac12EA(u')^2dx\) (split the integral where \(A\) changes), force potential with the sign set by the load direction.
  3. \(\partial\mathcal P/\partial a_i = 0\) and solve.
  4. For “better or not?” questions: richer is better only if all admissible lower-order terms are kept.

Common slip Wrong sign when gravity acts against the \(x\)-axis.

Apr 2025 2aApr 2025 2bApr 2025 2cWeek 8 Ex. 1Week 8 Ex. 3

1Week 1 · notes

Governing equations

April 2025 · 1d · 1.5 ptsThe three sets of equations

To predict the displacements of a structure under applied forces we need three sets of equations. Name them and say which quantities each relates.

Model answer
  • Kinematic equations: displacements and strains.
  • Equilibrium equations: forces and stresses.
  • Constitutive equations (material laws): strains and stresses.
2Week 2 · notes

Strain tensors

January 2026 · 1a · 7 ptsFinding a constant from a change in angle

At \(P\), \(\mathbf E = \begin{bmatrix}3/2 & 0 & b\\ 0 & -b/3 & 0\\ b & 0 & 9/2\end{bmatrix}\) with \(b > 0\). Two directions \(\mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf N\) in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_3\), each at \(45^\circ\) to the axes and perpendicular to each other (see figure), make an angle \(\varphi\) after deformation with \(\cos\varphi = \tfrac35\). Find \(b\).

Model answer

\(\Phi = \pi/2\), so \(\cos\Phi = 0\). With \(\mathbf M = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}[1\;-1]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mathbf N = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}[-1\;-1]^{\mathsf T}\) in \((\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_3)\): \(2\mathbf M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E\mathbf N = E_{33} - E_{11} = 3\), \(E_M = \tfrac12(E_{11} - 2E_{13} + E_{33}) = 3 - b\), \(E_N = 3 + b\).

\[ \cos\varphi = \frac{3}{\sqrt{7 - 2b}\,\sqrt{7 + 2b}} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{49 - 4b^2}} = \frac35 \;\Rightarrow\; b = \sqrt6. \]

April 2025 · 1a · 12.25 ptsPlacement from a gauge and an angle

A square block (side \(L\), corners 1–4) undergoes \(x = aX + bY\), \(y = cX + dY\), with no small-strain assumption. In the figure, edge 1–4 stays on the \(y\)-axis and corner 2 stays at \(x = L\). A gauge at the centre at \(45^\circ\) reads \(E_1 = \tfrac49\), and the corner angle \(\Phi = \pi/2\) at point 1 becomes \(\varphi\) with \(\cos\varphi = \tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\). Find \(a, b, c, d\) and the in-plane Green–Lagrange strains.

Model answer

\(a = 1\), \(b = 0\), \(c = \tfrac13\), \(d = \tfrac43\). With \(\mathbf F = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\ 1/3 & 4/3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf E = \tfrac12(\mathbf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf F - \mathbf I)\): \(E_{XX} = \tfrac1{18}\), \(E_{YY} = \tfrac7{18}\), \(E_{XY} = \tfrac29\). Check: \(E_M = \tfrac12(\tfrac1{18} + \tfrac49 + \tfrac7{18}) = \tfrac49\) ✓.

April 2026 · 1a · 10.25 ptsChoosing a strain gauge setup

A thin body has \(u_X = X - b\tfrac{XY}{L}\), \(u_Y = aX + Y\) (infinitesimal strain). At \(P\) (\(X = L/3\), \(Y = L/2\)) a two-gauge setup reads \(\epsilon_1 = \tfrac58\), \(\epsilon_2 = \tfrac34\). Choose setup A, B or C to find \(a\) and \(b\), explain why the others fail, and find \(a\) and \(b\).

a) Which setup?

Model answer

\(\epsilon_{XX} = 1 - \tfrac b2\), \(\epsilon_{YY} = 1\), \(\epsilon_{XY} = \tfrac12(a - \tfrac b3)\). Setup B: gauge 1 at \(30^\circ\) from \(\mathbf e_X\) gives \(\tfrac34\epsilon_{XX} + \tfrac14 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\epsilon_{XY} = \tfrac58\); gauge 2 at \(45^\circ\) gives \(\tfrac12(\epsilon_{XX} + 1) + \epsilon_{XY} = \tfrac34\). Solving: \(\epsilon_{XY} = 0\), \(\epsilon_{XX} = \tfrac12\), so \(b = 1\) and \(a = \tfrac13\).

January 2025 · 1c · 9.75 ptsTwo gauges, two constants

A thin structure (plane of \(\mathbf e_x, \mathbf e_z\)) has \(u_x = x + \alpha z\), \(u_z = \beta\tfrac{z^2}{W} - z\). At \(Q = [\tfrac L2\;\;0\;\;\tfrac W2]\) two gauges read \(\epsilon_1 = 2\), \(\epsilon_2 = \tfrac12\). Choose the configuration (A, B or C) that determines \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), find them, and give the in-plane strains.

a) Which configuration?

Model answer

\(\epsilon_{xx} = 1\), \(\epsilon_{zz} = \beta - 1\), \(\epsilon_{xz} = \tfrac\alpha2\). Gauge 2 along \(\mathbf e_z\): \(\beta - 1 = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow \beta = \tfrac32\). Gauge 1 at \(45^\circ\): \(\tfrac12(1 + \alpha + \tfrac12) = 2 \Rightarrow \alpha = \tfrac52\). Strains: \(\epsilon_{xx} = 1\), \(\epsilon_{zz} = \tfrac12\), \(\epsilon_{xz} = \tfrac54\).

April 2026 · 1c · 5.5 ptsMeaning of the off-diagonal strains

  • For large strain, what does \(E_{XY}\) represent? Words and equation.
  • When is infinitesimal strain theory valid?
  • For infinitesimal strain, what does \(\epsilon_{XY}\) represent, and how does it differ from the large-strain case?
Model answer

\(E_{XY}\) measures the change in angle between two line elements originally along \(\mathbf e_X\) and \(\mathbf e_Y\): \(\cos\varphi_{XY} = \tfrac{2E_{XY}}{\sqrt{1 + 2E_{XX}}\sqrt{1 + 2E_{YY}}}\). Infinitesimal strain is valid for small deformations and small rotations. Then \(\epsilon_{XY}\) gives the change in angle directly: \(\gamma_{XY} = 2\epsilon_{XY}\), a linear relation without the stretch terms of the large-strain formula.

3Week 3 · notes

Stress measures

April 2025 · 1b · 7.25 ptsShear stress on a cut

The block is in plane strain with \(\nu = 0.3\). At \(Q\), \(\boldsymbol\sigma = E\begin{bmatrix}1 & a & 0\\ a & 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & a+b\end{bmatrix}\). A straight cut runs from \((0, \tfrac L3)\) to \((L, \tfrac{2L}3)\). On the facet of the bottom part at \(Q\), the shear stress vector is \(\boldsymbol\sigma_\tau = \tfrac{E}{2\sqrt{10}}[9\;\;3\;\;0]^{\mathsf T}\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).

Model answer

\(\mathbf n = \tfrac1{\sqrt{10}}[-1\;3\;0]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mathbf p = \tfrac{E}{\sqrt{10}}[3a - 1\;\;6 - a\;\;0]^{\mathsf T}\). With \(\mathbf t = \tfrac1{\sqrt{10}}[3\;1\;0]^{\mathsf T}\): \(\boldsymbol\sigma_\tau = (\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf t)\mathbf t = \tfrac{E(3 + 8a)}{10\sqrt{10}}[3\;1\;0]^{\mathsf T}\). Matching gives \(3 + 8a = 15\), so \(a = \tfrac32\). Plane strain: \(a + b = 0.3(1 + 2) = 0.9\), so \(b = -\tfrac35\).

4Week 4 · notes

Equilibrium equations

April 2026 · 1b · 6.75 ptsNormal stress and body force at a cut

In-plane stresses: \(\sigma_{XX} = \rho s\left(3\tfrac{XY}{L} - X + 2Y\right)\), \(\sigma_{YY} = \rho s\left(9\tfrac{X^2}{L} - 4Y\right)\), \(\sigma_{XY} = \rho s\left(-2\tfrac{Y^2}{L} + \tfrac X5\right)\). The body is cut along a line from \((\tfrac L3, L)\) to \((\tfrac{2L}3, 0)\); \(Q\) lies on the cut of the left part at \(Y = \tfrac L3\). Find the normal stress at \(Q\) and \(f_X, f_Y\) at \(Q\) for equilibrium.

Model answer

At \(Q = (\tfrac{5L}9, \tfrac L3)\): \(\sigma_{XX} = \tfrac23\rho sL\), \(\sigma_{YY} = \tfrac{13}9\rho sL\), \(\sigma_{XY} = -\tfrac19\rho sL\). With \(\mathbf n = \tfrac1{\sqrt{10}}[3\;1]^{\mathsf T}\): \(\sigma = \tfrac{9\sigma_{XX} + 6\sigma_{XY} + \sigma_{YY}}{10} = \tfrac{61}{90}\rho sL\).

\(\rho f_X = -\rho s\left(3\tfrac YL - 1 - 4\tfrac YL\right) \Rightarrow f_X = s(1 + \tfrac YL) = \tfrac43s\); \(\rho f_Y = -\rho s\left(\tfrac15 - 4\right) \Rightarrow f_Y = \tfrac{19}5s\).

January 2025 · 1b · 6.25 ptsConstants from volume equilibrium

In the plane of \(\mathbf e_x, \mathbf e_z\): \(\sigma_{xx} = \rho\left(a\tfrac{x^2}L + cz\right)\), \(\sigma_{zz} = \rho c(x + z)\), \(\sigma_{xz} = \rho\left(b\tfrac{xz}L + 2c\tfrac{z^2}W\right)\), with \(c = 1\). At \(P = [\tfrac L3\;\;0\;\;\tfrac W4]\), \(\rho\mathbf f = \rho[2\;\;0\;\;-3]^{\mathsf T}\). Find \(a\), \(b\) and the full stress tensor at \(P\) (plane stress).

Model answer

Along \(\mathbf e_z\): \(\tfrac{bW}{4L} + 1 - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow b = \tfrac{8L}W\). Along \(\mathbf e_x\): \(\tfrac23a + \tfrac13b + 1 + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -\tfrac92 - \tfrac{4L}W\).

\[ \boldsymbol\sigma_P = \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{xx} & 0 & \sigma_{xz}\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ \sigma_{xz} & 0 & \sigma_{zz}\end{bmatrix}, \quad \sigma_{xx} = \rho\left(-\tfrac L2 - \tfrac{4L^2}{9W} + \tfrac W4\right), \quad \sigma_{zz} = \rho\left(\tfrac L3 + \tfrac W4\right), \quad \sigma_{xz} = \rho\left(\tfrac{2L}3 + \tfrac W8\right). \]

January 2025 · 1d · 4.5 ptsBoundary conditions on two edges

With \(\theta = 30^\circ\), the right edge carries \(2f\) and the front edge carries \(f\) at \(\varphi = 60^\circ\) to the horizontal (see figure). Write the equilibrium equations at both edges.

Model answer

Right edge: \(\mathbf n = \tfrac12[1\;0\;\sqrt3]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mathbf q = [0\;0\;2f]^{\mathsf T}\): \(\tfrac12\sigma_{xx} + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sigma_{xz} = 0\) and \(\tfrac12\sigma_{xz} + \tfrac{\sqrt3}2\sigma_{zz} = 2f\).

Front edge: \(\mathbf n = [-1\;0\;0]^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mathbf q = -\tfrac f2[\sqrt3\;0\;1]^{\mathsf T}\): \(\sigma_{xx} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2f\), \(\sigma_{xz} = \tfrac f2\).

January 2026 · 1c · 4 ptsStress state from a surface load

A force per unit area \(s\) acts at \(45^\circ\) on a small sloped face at \(P\) (zoom: vertical side \(\sqrt2h\), horizontal side \(h\)). Also \(\sigma_{11} - \sigma_{33} = -\sqrt3s\). Find the in-plane stresses at \(P\).

⚠ Possible mistake in the official solution

The answers here follow the workout: \(\sigma_{11} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}s\), \(\sigma_{33} = \sigma_{13} = \sqrt3(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}2)s\). These values don’t satisfy the workout’s own first two equations. Solving the same three equations gives \(\sigma_{11} = -\sqrt{\tfrac32}\,s\) and \(\sigma_{33} = \sigma_{13} = \sqrt3(1 - \tfrac{\sqrt2}2)s\). Ask your instructor before relying on it.

Model answer

With \(\mathbf n = \tfrac1{\sqrt3}[\sqrt2\;1]^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\mathbf q = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}s[-1\;1]^{\mathsf T}\) in \((\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_3)\):

\[ \tfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}\sigma_{11} + \tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sigma_{13} = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}2s, \qquad \tfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}\sigma_{13} + \tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sigma_{33} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2s, \qquad \sigma_{11} - \sigma_{33} = -\sqrt3s. \]

Solution sheet: \(\sigma_{11} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}\,s\), \(\sigma_{33} = \sigma_{13} = \sqrt3\left(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)s\).

5Week 5 · notes

Constitutive equations

January 2025 · 1a · 2 ptsAssumption for a 2D model

A thin structure (\(T \ll L\), \(T \ll W\)) is loaded in the plane of \(\mathbf e_x\) and \(\mathbf e_z\). Which assumption allows a 2D model, why, and what does \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) look like in its principal directions?

Which assumption?

Model answer

Plane stress: thin along \(\mathbf e_y\) and loaded only in the plane of \(\mathbf e_x, \mathbf e_z\). In principal directions, \(\boldsymbol\sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_x, 0, \sigma_z)\): one principal stress is zero.

January 2026 · 1b · 11.5 ptsWriting the strong form

A body thin along \(\mathbf e_2\) is supported on \(a_u\) (\(\mathbf u = \mathbf 0\)), loaded by \(\mathbf q\) on \(a_q\) and by \(\rho\mathbf f\) in its volume, all in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_3\). Which assumption allows a 2D model, and what is the full strong form for the in-plane displacements?

Model answer

Plane stress: thin along \(\mathbf e_2\), loaded only in the plane of \(\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_3\).

Unknowns: \(u_1, u_3\); \(\epsilon_{11}, \epsilon_{33}, \epsilon_{13}\); \(\sigma_{11}, \sigma_{33}, \sigma_{13}\).

\[ \textbf{Kinematic:}\quad \epsilon_{11} = \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial x_1}, \quad \epsilon_{33} = \frac{\partial u_3}{\partial x_3}, \quad \epsilon_{13} = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial u_1}{\partial x_3} + \frac{\partial u_3}{\partial x_1}\right) \]
\[ \textbf{Equilibrium:}\quad \frac{\partial\sigma_{11}}{\partial x_1} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{13}}{\partial x_3} + \rho f_1 = 0, \quad \frac{\partial\sigma_{13}}{\partial x_1} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{33}}{\partial x_3} + \rho f_3 = 0 \]
\[ \textbf{Constitutive:}\quad \epsilon_{11} = \frac1E(\sigma_{11} - \nu\sigma_{33}), \quad \epsilon_{33} = \frac1E(-\nu\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{33}), \quad \epsilon_{13} = \frac{1+\nu}E\sigma_{13} \]
\[ \textbf{Boundary:}\quad \sigma_{11}n_1 + \sigma_{13}n_3 = q_1,\;\; \sigma_{13}n_1 + \sigma_{33}n_3 = q_3 \text{ on } a_q; \qquad u_1 = u_3 = 0 \text{ on } a_u. \]

April 2025 · 1c · 1.5 ptsWhich curves are elastic?

Describe the assumption of elasticity, and say for each stress–strain curve A, B, C whether it belongs to an elastic material.

Select the elastic curves.

Model answer

Elastic: the behaviour is reversible; when loads are removed the material returns to its initial configuration and no net work is done over a loading–unloading cycle. A is elastic (linear), C is elastic (nonlinear), B is not: unloading follows a different path.

6Week 6 · notes

Principle of virtual work

January 2025 · 2a · 4.25 ptsRelating the virtual angles

Two rigid bars (length \(L\) at angle \(\theta\), length \(2L\) at angle \(\gamma\)) meet at point 3, where a box \(M\) hangs. Point 4 is pinned, point 2 slides along \(\mathbf e_X\), and a spring \(k\) connects 1 and 2 (unloaded at \(\theta_0, \gamma_0\)). Find \(f[\theta, \gamma]\) such that \(\delta\theta = f\,\delta\gamma\).

Model answer

\(\Delta y_{24} = 2L\cos\gamma - L\sin\theta\) is constant, so \(-2L\sin\gamma\,\delta\gamma - L\cos\theta\,\delta\theta = 0\) and \(f[\theta, \gamma] = -\tfrac{2\sin\gamma}{\cos\theta}\).

January 2025 · 2b · 11 ptsMass for equilibrium

Same mechanism. Compute the external and internal virtual work in terms of \(\delta\gamma\) (keep \(f[\theta, \gamma]\) as is) and find \(M\) at equilibrium.

Model answer

External: the box hangs below point 3, so \(\delta y_M = -2L\sin\gamma\,\delta\gamma\) and \(\delta W_E = 2MgL\sin\gamma\,\delta\gamma\).

Internal: spring elongation \(\Delta\ell = -2L\sin\gamma - L\cos\theta + 2L\sin\gamma_0 + L\cos\theta_0\), so \(\delta\Delta\ell = (-2L\cos\gamma + L\sin\theta\, f)\,\delta\gamma\) and \(\delta W_I = k\,\Delta\ell\,\delta\Delta\ell\).

\[ M = \frac{kL}{g}\left(2\sin\gamma + \cos\theta - 2\sin\gamma_0 - \cos\theta_0\right)\left(\frac1{\tan\gamma} - \frac12\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin\gamma}\,f[\theta, \gamma]\right). \]

January 2025 · 2d · 2.75 ptsWhy reactions do no virtual work

Which assumption on the virtual displacements makes the reactions do no virtual work, what does it require, and what does it imply for this mechanism?

Model answer

Kinematically admissible virtual displacements: they keep the body continuous and satisfy the kinematic boundary conditions. Here: \(\delta u_x = \delta u_y = 0\) at points 1 and 4, and \(\delta u_y = 0\) at point 2.

January 2026 · 2b · 7 ptsA pushed springboard

A springboard: bar 1–3 is fixed; bar 2–6 (angle \(\varphi\)) is pinned at 2 (at height \(L\)) and connected at 5 (at \(2L\) from 2) to bar 5–7 (length \(2L\), angle \(\theta\)), which slides along \(\mathbf e_x\) at 7. A force \(F\) at \(60^\circ\) pushes point 7. Find \(f[\varphi, \theta]\) with \(\delta\theta = f\,\delta\varphi\), and the external virtual work of \(F\) in terms of \(\delta\varphi\).

Model answer

\(L + 2L\sin\varphi = 2L\sin\theta \Rightarrow 2L\cos\varphi\,\delta\varphi = 2L\cos\theta\,\delta\theta\), so \(f = \tfrac{\cos\varphi}{\cos\theta}\).

\(x_7 = 2L\cos\varphi + 2L\cos\theta\), the horizontal component \(F_x = F/2\) points left: \(\delta W_E = -F_x\,\delta x_7 = FL(\sin\varphi\,\delta\varphi + \sin\theta\,\delta\theta) = FL(\sin\varphi + \tan\theta\cos\varphi)\,\delta\varphi\).

April 2026 · 2a · 16.25 ptsA press mechanism

Three rigid pieces and a spring \(k\) (unloaded at \(\alpha_0, \gamma_0\)): the angled top piece (constant bend \(\beta\), arms \(L\) and \(2L\), angle \(\alpha\) to the vertical) is pinned at 5; the middle piece (\(2L\), angle \(\gamma\) to the horizontal) connects it to the bottom piece, which slides vertically at 1 and 2. A force \(F\) acts at point 4 at \(120^\circ\) to the horizontal. Find \(f[\alpha, \gamma]\) with \(\delta\gamma = f\,\delta\alpha\) and the equilibrium equation by virtual work.

Model answer

\(f[\alpha, \gamma] = -\tfrac{\cos\alpha}{2\sin\gamma}\). Equilibrium (solution sheet):

\[ \frac F2\left(\cos\alpha - 2\cos(\beta - \alpha)\right) - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}F\left(\sin\alpha + 2\sin(\beta - \alpha)\right) = -kL\left(\cos\alpha + 2\sin\gamma - \cos\alpha_0 - 2\sin\gamma_0\right)\left(\sin\alpha + 2\cos\alpha\cot\gamma\right). \]

January 2026 · 2c · 5 ptsAdmissible displacements and assumptions

  • What is the difference between compatible and kinematically admissible displacements?
  • Draw the admissible displacement direction at each joint of the springboard (a cross if none).
  • Which two extra assumptions does minimum potential energy need compared with virtual work?
Model answer

Compatible displacements keep the structure continuous; kinematically admissible ones are compatible and satisfy the kinematic boundary conditions.

Joints 1, 2, 3: no displacement (bar 1–3 is held at both ends). Joints 4, 5, 6: perpendicular to bar 2–6, which rotates about 2. Joint 7: horizontal.

Conservative material: unloaded, it returns to its initial configuration; no net work over a load–unload cycle. Conservative forces: their work is independent of the path taken.

7Week 7 · notes

Minimum potential energy

January 2026 · 2a · 10.5 ptsSpring stiffness for a mouse on a springboard

A mouse \(m\) sits at the tip 6 of bar 2–6 (\(3L\) from 2). The spring \(k\) runs from 3 (at height \(2L\) above 1) to 4 (\(L\) from 2 along the bar) and is unloaded at \(\varphi_0\). Using minimum potential energy, find \(k\) for equilibrium.

Model answer

Spring length \(\ell = \sqrt{(L - L\sin\varphi)^2 + (L\cos\varphi)^2} = L\sqrt{2(1 - \sin\varphi)}\), so \(\mathcal U = kL^2\left(\sqrt{1 - \sin\varphi} - \sqrt{1 - \sin\varphi_0}\right)^2\). Mouse height \(h = L + 3L\sin\varphi\), so \(\mathcal F = 3mgL(\sin\varphi - \sin\varphi_0)\).

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal P}{\partial\varphi} = -kL^2\,\frac{\sqrt{1-\sin\varphi} - \sqrt{1-\sin\varphi_0}}{\sqrt{1-\sin\varphi}}\cos\varphi + 3mgL\cos\varphi = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; k = \frac{3mg}{L}\,\frac{\sqrt{1-\sin\varphi}}{\sqrt{1-\sin\varphi} - \sqrt{1-\sin\varphi_0}}. \]

January 2025 · 2c · 4.5 ptsA cat on the mechanism

A cat of mass \(C\) sits on the \(2L\) bar at \(\tfrac{3L}2\) from point 4. Find its force potential and the variation in terms of \(\delta\gamma\).

Model answer

\(\mathcal F = Cg(y_C - y_{C,0}) = \tfrac32CgL(\cos\gamma - \cos\gamma_0)\); \(\delta\mathcal F = -\tfrac32CgL\sin\gamma\,\delta\gamma\).

April 2026 · 2b · 3.75 ptsForce potential of a horizontal force

A force \(R\) acts horizontally halfway along the middle piece of the press. Give its force potential and its variation in terms of \(\delta\alpha\) and \(\delta\gamma\).

Model answer

\(\mathcal F = RL(\cos\gamma - \cos\gamma_0)\); \(\delta\mathcal F = -RL\sin\gamma\,\delta\gamma\) (no \(\delta\alpha\) term).

April 2026 · 2c · 2.5 ptsAssumptions for minimum potential energy

The press now carries a mass \(M\) at point 4. Name the two assumptions behind minimum potential energy and say what they require here.

Model answer

Conservative material: rigid pieces (no deformation) and a linear spring. Conservative forces: gravity is conservative, and the joints and supports are frictionless.

8Week 8 · notes

Rayleigh–Ritz method

April 2025 · 2a · 2.5 ptsMaking a trial admissible

A nest structure (bar, length \(L\), fixed at \(x = 0\)) gets the trial \(u^{\text{trial}} = \alpha\sin\left(\pi(\tfrac xL - \tfrac12)\right) + \beta\cos\left(\pi(\tfrac xL - \tfrac12)\right)\). Make it kinematically admissible.

Which coefficient must vanish?

Model answer

Sine and cosine are continuous. \(u[0] = -\alpha = 0\), so \(u^{\text{trial}} = \beta\cos\left(\pi(\tfrac xL - \tfrac12)\right)\).

April 2025 · 2b · 15 ptsA linear trial for the nest

The area grows linearly from \(A/2\) at \(x = 0\) to \(A\) at \(x = \tfrac{3L}4\), then stays \(A\). A stork of mass \(B\) loads the top (\(x = L\)) as a point load; packages of mass \(C\) load \(\tfrac{3L}4 \le x \le L\) uniformly. Gravity acts downward (against \(x\)). With \(u^{\text{trial}} = \alpha x\), find \(\mathcal P\) and \(\alpha\).

Model answer
\[ \mathcal P = \frac{13}{32}EAL\,\alpha^2 + BgL\,\alpha + \frac78CgL\,\alpha, \qquad \alpha = -\frac{16g}{13EA}\left(B + \frac78C\right), \qquad u^{\text{trial}} = -\frac{16g}{13EA}\left(B + \frac78C\right)x. \]

April 2025 · 2c · 5 ptsWill a richer trial help?

a) Does \(\alpha x + \beta x^2\) give a better approximation than \(\alpha x\)?

b) Does \(\beta x^2\) alone give a better approximation than \(\alpha x + \beta x^2\)?

What to know by heart

These results show up throughout the exercises but aren’t printed on the formula sheet.

ResultExpressionWeek
Green–Lagrange in matrix form\(\mathbf E = \tfrac12\left(\tfrac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X} + \tfrac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}^{\mathsf T}\right) + \tfrac12\tfrac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}^{\mathsf T}\tfrac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial\mathbf X}\)1
Cauchy strain\(\epsilon_{ij} = \tfrac12\left(\tfrac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} + \tfrac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right)\)2

Normal and shear stress\(\sigma = \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p,\quad \tau^2 = \mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p - \sigma^2\)3

Plane strain\(\epsilon_{i3} = 0,\quad \sigma_{33} = \nu(\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{22})\)5
